utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Good morning, everyone.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Good morning.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Would the witness take the solemn declaration, please.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I solemnly declare that I will speak the truth, the whole truth, and nothing but the truth.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Thank you. Please be seated.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Would the Chamber move into private session briefly.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Yes. Good morning, Mr. Davidovic. I understand that you are willing to testify in this case publicly, without any protective measures.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Good morning. Yes, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Thank you very much. Yes, Ms. West.

utterances.speaker: MS. WEST
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. President.

utterances.speaker: MS. WEST
utterances.text: Sir, can you just tell us your full name for the record.

utterances.speaker: SRBISLAV DAVIDOVIC
utterances.text: Srbislav Davidovic.

utterances.speaker: MS. WEST
utterances.text: Mr. Davidovic, where were you born?

utterances.speaker: SRBISLAV DAVIDOVIC
utterances.text: I was born in Bratunac, in Bosnia.

utterances.speaker: MS. WEST
utterances.text: And where do you live now?

utterances.speaker: SRBISLAV DAVIDOVIC
utterances.text: I live in Bratunac.

utterances.speaker: MS. WEST
utterances.text: Mr. Davidovic, can you confirm that you had an opportunity to listen to your testimony in the Popovic case and that with the exception of a few corrections that we'll discuss in a moment, it accurately reflected your evidence to that Court?

utterances.speaker: SRBISLAV DAVIDOVIC
utterances.text: Yes. I had the opportunity to listen to this, and I agree with it.

utterances.speaker: MS. WEST
utterances.text: And there were two corrections you wanted to make on transcript page 9183 where you spoke about working at the people's university in Bratunac until the beginning of the war in 1992, but in the transcript it said 1991. So that correction should be changing the year to 1992; is that right?

utterances.speaker: SRBISLAV DAVIDOVIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. WEST
utterances.text: And the second correction is transcript page 9184. In describing the duties of the Executive Board, you indicated it was logistics support to the Bratunac Brigade, not logistics brigade to the Bratunac Brigade as was mistakenly reflected in the transcript; is that right?

utterances.speaker: SRBISLAV DAVIDOVIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. WEST
utterances.text: And other than those inaccuracies, was the Popovic testimony accurate and reflected your evidence?

utterances.speaker: SRBISLAV DAVIDOVIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. WEST
utterances.text: And if you were asked about the same issues today here in court, would you provide the same information?

utterances.speaker: SRBISLAV DAVIDOVIC
utterances.text: I'm sure I would provide the same information. The essence would be the same. Now, whether the exact words would be the same, that's another matter, but the essence would be the same.

utterances.speaker: MS. WEST
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MS. WEST
utterances.text: Mr. President, we move to admit Popovic testimony which is 65 ter 22305A, and there's only one associated exhibit.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Which was a pseudonym sheet.

utterances.speaker: MS. WEST
utterances.text: Correct. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Both will be admitted.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: As Exhibit D4371 and D4372 respectively, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: The another -- the other associate exhibit which was admitted yesterday, it was Ms. Sutherland, I take it, I asked whether similar ones were already admitted, and I was informed by the Registry that the similar document with respect to other municipalities or other localities were admitted but not in relation to Srebrenica. I put it just for the record. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: The -- the pseudonym sheet now that all the protective measures have been rescinded shouldn't be put under seal.

utterances.speaker: MS. WEST
utterances.text: I would say no.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: And we have a redacted or public -- private session amongst the transcript. Those will be -- can be admitted in full, in -- publicly. Could you double-check?

utterances.speaker: MS. WEST
utterances.text: I will.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MS. WEST
utterances.text: Mr. Davidovic, I just have a few questions for you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Would you like to tender some summary of his evidence?

utterances.speaker: MS. WEST
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. President.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: For the public.

utterances.speaker: MS. WEST
utterances.text: The witness was employed as director of the people's university in Bratunac from 1984 till 1992. From October 1994 to March 1997, the witness worked as president of the Bratunac municipality Executive Board and one of his tasks was to provide logistics support to the Bratunac Brigade during the war. On July 9th, 1995, the witness visited the -- the 3rd Battalion of the Bratunac Brigade located in Pribicevac with a purpose to see what was the logistical situation there. And on the 11th of July, the witness returned to the 3rd Battalion where he had a brief unpleasant encounter with General Mladic who ordered the witness to go to the command post. On his way to the command post, the witness came across Miroslav Deronjic, president of the Municipal Board of the SDS. Later that day, the witness was notified from Deronjic to attend a meeting at the Bratunac Brigade command at 8.00 a.m. on the following morning. On July 12th the following morning, the witness went to the Bratunac Brigade command where General Mladic asked the witness to attend the third Hotel Fontana meeting at 10.00 a.m. that morning, only two hours later. The witness went to the third Hotel Fontana meeting and at that meeting the witness learned that the Muslim population decided to leave the region, although General Mladic, the witness indicated, offered them the possibility to stay in the region under the condition that the army hand over their weapons and that those who bloodied their hands and committed crimes against the Serbian people would be prosecuted. During the meeting, Mladic also told the Muslims that "they could either survive or disappear." Later that day, the witness went to Potocari and helped distribute some of the supplies to the Muslim refugees, and during his visit to Potocari, the witness recognised several people whom he knew among the refugees, and he was able to help some of them. After the witness left Potocari and returned to Bratunac later that afternoon, he went to his office, and in the evening he saw at least six buses parked in the town and also learned of 20 to 25 buses parked elsewhere in the town. Each of them was filled with Muslim men. The witness knew that the buses spent the night in Bratunac, but before the morning, they left Bratunac. On the 14th of July, around 7.00 a.m., two men who were the directors of the co-operative, the agricultural co-operative in Kravica visited the witness in his office. He told the witness about mass killings of Muslims in the Kravica warehouse which occurred in the afternoon of July 13th. Later that morning, around 9.30, the witness was called to the SDS office. When he arrived there, he met an officer who introduced himself as Beara. Beara invited the witness to another office to talk to two other officers whom the witness did not know, but one of them he indicated was a colonel and the other was a lieutenant-colonel. These two officers questioned the witness about obtaining construction equipment, and the witness told them about -- about construction machine called a ULT which was owned by the Brickworks factory and it was used for loading. He also told them about a smaller machine called a SKIP which was owned by the utilities company and it was use for digging. They asked the witness to provide the ULT machine and the witness contacted the director of the Brickworks factory. Although the officers did not tell the witness the reason why they needed the equipment, he assumed, the witness assumed, that the equipment would be used for digging graves.

utterances.speaker: MS. WEST
utterances.text: Mr. Davidovic, in the Popovic case you had testified regarding a meeting on July 14th at 9.30 in the morning at the SDS office and you testified that at that meeting was an individual named Beara and two other officers and you didn't know their names. Can you tell the Trial Chamber what those two officers asked from you.

utterances.speaker: SRBISLAV DAVIDOVIC
utterances.text: These two men asked me whether there were any construction machines in Bratunac that can be used for digging and loading. I knew that our brickworks had a machine like that. The machine was called the ULT, and I said that there was one like that at the Brickworks factory, and I said there was a smaller one called a skip that was at the public utilities company. They asked me whether we can make that machine available. I said that I'd discuss it with the director whether it was in proper working order, and if it was, then we would make it available to them. However, I'm not sure that we could also make available a person who could operate that machine. I said that for the following reason: I know the machine operator who worked on that machine in 1992, and that was a very unpleasant and painstaking job. That is what I thought of, and in a way I tried to protect this man, this operator. One of these two officers cautioned me quite sternly that it was not for me to say who could and who could not operate that machine, and I said I'm sorry, this was just an observation of mine. It is not binding in any way, and then I left the office with a promise that I would call the manager of that company and that they should establish further contact with him. Now, whether they did take that machine or not I don't know, and I did not seek any further information. That would be it briefly, what happened at that meeting. On my way out, I said hello to Colonel Beara -- or I said good-bye to Colonel Beara in the next -- in the office next door, and I never saw these people again.

utterances.speaker: MS. WEST
utterances.text: Did you know why those two officers wanted the machine?

utterances.speaker: SRBISLAV DAVIDOVIC
utterances.text: They did not tell me why they wanted the machine. However, since those two managers from the agricultural co-operative told me at 7.00 that morning what had happened in Kravica on the previous day in the afternoon, my conclusion was that most probably they needed the machine for sanitisation and evacuation of persons that had been executed within Kravica. I mean, that was my very own conclusion. That's not what they said.

utterances.speaker: MS. WEST
utterances.text: And do you know where those two men were from?

utterances.speaker: SRBISLAV DAVIDOVIC
utterances.text: I don't know. I assume that they were from the Drina Corps. Knowing that Colonel Beara was the security man at the Drina Corps, I had assumed that this man had come with him, that he had brought them, and that they were all from the Drina Corps.

utterances.speaker: MS. WEST
utterances.text: Thank you, sir.

utterances.speaker: MS. WEST
utterances.text: Mr. President, I don't have any more questions.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Thank you. Mr. Davidovic, your testimony in the Popovic et al. case has been admitted in this case in lieu of your testimony in chief, and that you will be further asked by Mr. Karadzic in his cross-examination. Yes, Mr. Karadzic.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you. Good morning, Excellencies. Good morning to all.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Good morning, Mr. Davidovic.

utterances.speaker: SRBISLAV DAVIDOVIC
utterances.text: Good morning, Mr. President.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: I'm following the interpretation to see when it's over, and if you have the transcript, then you can see when the interpretation is over, and we should pause. And I would like to thank you for the video-conference -- the video meeting we held, and I hope that it will make it possible for us to finish this cross-examination on time, and thank you once again.

utterances.speaker: SRBISLAV DAVIDOVIC
utterances.text: What I have here is English. No, I haven't got anything in Serbian yet.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Yes, it will in English all along, but when the typing stops, that means that you can speak then.

utterances.speaker: SRBISLAV DAVIDOVIC
utterances.text: I'll do my best.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Thank you. So before the elections in 1990, you were in a party of the political left, and you were not a member of the SDS; right?

utterances.speaker: SRBISLAV DAVIDOVIC
utterances.text: That's right. The Social Democratic Party.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Thank you. However, in 1994, isn't that right, you were elected head of the local government, actually of the Executive Council, which is the municipal government, not because you were a member of the SDS, because you were not a member of the SDS at that point in time; isn't that right?

utterances.speaker: SRBISLAV DAVIDOVIC
utterances.text: That is right.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Rather, you were elected as a professional.

utterances.speaker: SRBISLAV DAVIDOVIC
utterances.text: It wasn't party affiliation that was decisive.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Thank you. I would like to ask you to tell us as briefly as possible how you viewed developments in Bratunac after the elections and at the very beginning of the war. Do you agree that the Party of Democratic Action and the Serb Democratic Party had won there and that they shared power according to the model that prevailed throughout Bosnia-Herzegovina?

utterances.speaker: SRBISLAV DAVIDOVIC
utterances.text: Both of these parties had won. The SDS won the votes of the Serb people; the SDA won the votes of the Muslim people. My party, unfortunately, remained as a minority party, and quite a minority at that. So it was those two parties that shared power, the SDA and the SDS.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Thank you. Did we agree that this was a good custom in our political life even in the days of the Communists, that power should be shared on the basis of some kind of ethnic structure? For example, if the president of the municipality is a Muslim, then the Serb would be President of the Executive Board, and there would also be that kind of sharing of high offices in the police, and this continued after 1990, as well; right?

utterances.speaker: SRBISLAV DAVIDOVIC
utterances.text: That's right. In the League of Communists before the war, ethnic affiliation was taken into account. If a particular office was held by a Serb, by way of an analogy, a Muslim would hold another office. Those were the posts that were filled that way. The same went for company managers, half/half. Half were Muslims, half why Serbs, but this was taken into account, ethnic affiliation. And that continued after the multi-party elections, after these two parties won the election.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Thank you. Both Serbs and Muslims had the chance of voting for other parties too. For example, Serbs were in some other political parties as well, just as the Muslims were, whereas the Muslims had a purely Muslim Bosniak organisation. So that was not the only option, right?

utterances.speaker: SRBISLAV DAVIDOVIC
utterances.text: No, it wasn't.

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: Interpreter's note: Could all other microphones be switched off. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] However, more or less, people voted in accordance with their ethnic affiliation.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Thank you. Can we say that for a considerable amount of time Bratunac functioned well? Well, I don't mean you, the opposition. But in terms of ethnic harmony, for a while everything seemed to be fine.

utterances.speaker: SRBISLAV DAVIDOVIC
utterances.text: Well, if we can put it that way, at first there was love between these two parties, but later on when the slope became slippery, if I can put it that way, there was no love left.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Thank you. Can we agree that tensions rose sometime in the summer of 1991 when Slovenia and Croatia declared independence? And before that, as for that declaration of independence in the Assembly of Bosnia-Herzegovina there were further tensions.

utterances.speaker: SRBISLAV DAVIDOVIC
utterances.text: That's right. As tensions went up in Slovenia and Croatia, this was reflected in a major way in the security situation in Bosnia-Herzegovina, Bratunac included.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Thank you. The Muslim Bosniak organisation of Adil Zulfikarpasic and Muhamed Filipovic did not make it into municipal parliament or did they with a couple of delegates?

utterances.speaker: SRBISLAV DAVIDOVIC
utterances.text: I believe they didn't. I think it was only the SDA and the SDS who actually won seats.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Thank you. Do you recall that in the summer of 1991, Zulfikarpasic and Muhamed Filipovic proposed an historic Serbian -- Serb-Muslim agreement whereby Bosnia would remain in Yugoslavia as an equal republic but that they should move away from any concept of regionalisation in Bosnia and Herzegovina?

utterances.speaker: SRBISLAV DAVIDOVIC
utterances.text: Yes, I do recall that. That was the option for Yugoslavia as well, and the late Izetbegovic was offered to be the first president of such a new Yugoslavia.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Thank you. Is it correct that the first crisis followed by unrest erupted sometime in late August, early September, when the JNA wanted to remove their records in order to be able to send call-ups for mobilisation?

utterances.speaker: SRBISLAV DAVIDOVIC
utterances.text: That's correct. That was sometime in late summer or early fall, if I recall that correctly, when the -- when members of the army came from Tuzla to take over the records from the Ministry of Defence in Bratunac. At that time, there was unrest in the town. The Muslims did not want this to happen, and at least 10.000 people gathered in the town itself, and the atmosphere was very tense. However, there was no spark, to put it that way, but the records were not removed from Bratunac at the time, the military records. They remained there.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Thank you. Do we agree that that was, in fact, the crucial point where the Muslims and the Serbs parted their ways, because the Serbs were in favour of Yugoslavia and the federal army, whereas the Muslims already in late summer of that year by this action demonstrated that they were not willing to side with the JNA and that they were going to oppose the Yugoslavia as it was?

utterances.speaker: SRBISLAV DAVIDOVIC
utterances.text: I believe that the concord between these two parties in fact broke down at that point in time for good. The Muslim people, for the most part, ceased responding to the call-up, mobilisation call-up, for the JNA. Some people still did. Some Muslims still did respond, but those families who sent their sons to the JNA were under pressure, and they were harassed by their neighbourhoods so that there were occasions where people returned from the army, and when the war broke out, the JNA ended up having very few Muslims in its ranks.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Thank you. The harassing that you mention, the harassing of the families of the people who responded to the call-ups, they were being harassed by Muslim extremists; correct?

utterances.speaker: SRBISLAV DAVIDOVIC
utterances.text: Yes. These were loyal citizens, loyal citizens of the former Yugoslavia and loyal to its army, and these people were harassed and maltreated by these extremists. And in the end many of them actually succumbed to this pressure in fear for their own safety and the safety of their children once they returned from the army, and, in fact, they pulled them out, in many cases, of the army.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Thank you. On the other hand, no one interfered with the families whose children went to Croatia to be clandestinely trained for the police or those who joined the ranks of the National Guards Corps, the ZNG, in Croatia.

utterances.speaker: SRBISLAV DAVIDOVIC
utterances.text: Well, there were people who went to Croatia. They were referred to as the Zengas. They went there for training, but what their numbers were, I don't know, but I do know that there were individuals who went to Croatia for training, and they were called Zengas, members of the ZNG.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Thank you. Does the Zenga actually mean, colloquially speaking, a member of the National Guards Corps in Croatia?

utterances.speaker: SRBISLAV DAVIDOVIC
utterances.text: Well, to tell you the truth, I don't really know the correct definition, but at the time, to us, that name seemed to be - well, how should I put it? - almost equal to the term "Ustasha." For Serbs, it was a very threatening term. I don't know how to put this right, but something to that effect.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Thank you. Is it correct that some of your colleague citizens who were in Croatian ranks committed some crimes and rapes, and that the victims of those crimes then surfaced in paramilitary forces at the beginning?

utterances.speaker: SRBISLAV DAVIDOVIC
utterances.text: Well, I recall the date, the 17th of April. This was the day when paramilitary groups appeared in Bratunac for the first time. Now, who they were or what they were, I did not know at the time. All I knew was they had come from Serbia, and once they arrived in Bratunac, the harassment and mistreatment and torture of the Muslim population began. There was some 15 men or so, and I recall this day -- can I go into detail? Can I explain this further?

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Yes, please go on.

utterances.speaker: SRBISLAV DAVIDOVIC
utterances.text: Well, that morning I left off for downtown Bratunac, around 8.00 in the morning. My house was on the outskirts. And on my way to the centre of town, I stopped by a greengrocer's which had been blown up the night before, and this greengrocer's was the property of an Albanian who had lived in Bratunac for many years. I knew the man, and I bought my vegetables and fruit in his green -- in his grocery store. So I stopped by him to exchange a few words and asked him what had happened. At that point a woman appeared. Her name was Sida, and she came crying towards us. And I asked her, What's the matter, Sida? Why are you crying? And she said, Oh, Buco - and that's my nickname. That's what everyone called me there - Buco, Bratunac is full of Chetniks, she says. What Chetniks? What are you saying. And then she says, Well, you don't know you've just coming from home, but when you get there, you'll see. And then I headed for the centre of town, that was some 200 metres further. When I arrived outside the department store, there was a group of people. A lot of people were gathered there, most of them Muslim, and then on the other side of the road was Hotel Fontana. And there, I saw some 15 uniformed men with automatic rifles. They were spread out on the terrace over 40 metres or so. That's how long the terrace was. In front of the department store I noticed Miroslav Deronjic, and then I asked him, Miroslav, who are those men? And he said, I don't know. Literally, that's what he said. He said, I don't know. Fuck it - my apologies for using this terminology, but I'm just quoting - when did they get here? I have no idea, just like you don't. Then, at the end, next to these uniformed men I see a man from Bratunac who joined them, and I said, Miroslav, please go and tell that man to remove himself. What is he going with them? And then he went and addressed this man. I suppose he told him, Just get lost. What are you doing there? And so I remember this. This was that first scene when volunteers appeared in Bratunac and when the fear and feeling of insecurity among the Muslims began and then increased, and then -- they were increasingly -- began moving out of Bratunac.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Thank you. Is it correct to say that this whole complex of events was fanned by the existence of Muslim extremists who were, as you told us, not in the town itself but in the surrounding villages?

utterances.speaker: SRBISLAV DAVIDOVIC
utterances.text: Well, there were no Muslim extremists in the town itself. I mean, the citizens of Bratunac itself, both Serb and Muslims, were loyal to one another. I think that it was the people from the rural areas, from the villages, the surrounding villages, Serbs or Muslims. I think that had they not come to Bratunac, war would never have broken out in Bratunac. What I'm trying to say is there were no extremists on either side in the town itself, and if there were some, that was negligible. It was very -- it would have been very easy to deal with them.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Thank you. However, is it correct that the villages, both Muslim and Serbs, were rather close to each other and that they were more or less purely defined as -- by ethnicity; correct?

utterances.speaker: SRBISLAV DAVIDOVIC
utterances.text: Well, yes, that's correct. The villages are close to one another, but they were ethnically clearly defined. They were not mixed villages. It was either a Serb village or a Muslim village. The mixing of ethnicities existed in the town self.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Thank you. Hranca as a Muslim concentration, was it very close, on the very outskirts of Bratunac, and then right next to Hranca was Glogovac with some 2.000 Muslim inhabitants and maybe two households of Serbs.

utterances.speaker: SRBISLAV DAVIDOVIC
utterances.text: That's correct. Glogova was ethnically pure, as was Hranca, and Glogova was a big Muslim village. They probably numbered some 2.000 inhabitants.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Thank you. You were not a member of the local government at the time. Is it true that Deronjic was not a member of the local government either at the time?

utterances.speaker: SRBISLAV DAVIDOVIC
utterances.text: That's -- well, I was not a member of the local government. I was busy with the local adult education centre. That's where I worked. And Deronjic was just the president of the local SDS. He did have a function, but that was at the regional level, not in the town itself. But he was not a member of the local government.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Thank you. So let's just go back to Deronjic. Was he a very prominent person, a professor, and for many years in opposition to the Communist regime, or, rather, a dissident?

utterances.speaker: SRBISLAV DAVIDOVIC
utterances.text: That's correct. Deronjic was a high-school teacher, a teacher of literature, and he was well known before the war as a person in opposition to the League of Communists.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Thank you. Is it correct that his reputation was based on his own conduct in Bratunac and that it was not something that was imposed by anyone from any side or outside of there, but, rather, it was his own actions?

utterances.speaker: SRBISLAV DAVIDOVIC
utterances.text: Well, he became a prominent member, or he came to the fore of the SDS by popular support. His father was well known as an Orthodox Communist, and even his mother was a Communist. Now, Deronjic was a next door neighbour, and I remember how surprised I was one morning when my father, I saw him getting dressed, getting ready to go out, so I asked him, Where are you going? He said, I'm going to Miroslav's Slava, a patron saint's day. I said, What's Slava? I mean, he doesn't -- you know, they don't celebrate that well. They began celebrating that now. When his father died, his mother --

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: Interpreter's correction: When his mother died.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] She was buried without a priest, and there was just a star on his -- on her grave, but then a few days later Miroslav went there and removed that far. This is -- and he brought a priest there in order to have a funeral, a proper funeral service. So what I'm trying to say is that he was a prominent opponent of the League of Communists, and that started before the war.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Thank you. Just on an aside, a question for you: Do you agree that these were the most crucial divisions that divided the Serb people? They were either Chetniks or Communists, and they -- in that sense, there were far more internecine conflicts than -- within the ethnicity, Serbs amongst themselves, rather than against other ethnicities?

utterances.speaker: SRBISLAV DAVIDOVIC
utterances.text: Well, we were a small community. We knew each other. We knew who belonged to what party, more or less. And I can tell you, for instance, that I was in trouble at the beginning of the war because I remained in the League of Communists. I did not choose to join the SDS. I wasn't under specific pressure from anyone, but people did hold it against me.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Thank you. Probably what you're referring to is you went -- I mean, that was how you were treated by some extremists but not by the authorities.

utterances.speaker: SRBISLAV DAVIDOVIC
utterances.text: That's correct, not by authorities.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Thank you. Now, please tell us, in view of the civilised conduct and mutual relationships between the Muslims and Serbs in Bratunac, can you tell us whether negotiations were underway, successful, to establish two municipalities in Bratunac, and is -- was that, in fact, the -- the main concern and the main substance of the political developments at the time?

utterances.speaker: SRBISLAV DAVIDOVIC
utterances.text: Well, that's what happened. Now, Deronjic was a next door neighbour, and I had frequent occasion to talk about this with him. He kept telling me that it was possible to have both a Serb and a municipal -- and a Muslim municipality in Bratunac. I did not believe that. I told him, Miroslav, I don't think that's possible. He kept insisting and tried to convince me that it was possible, but in the end that's indeed what happened. First, they divided the police so that the Muslim police remained in the then police building. The Serbs established their own police station on the premises of an elementary school, but that did not last long.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Thank you. Am I right if I say that part of the town itself in some Serb villages were the Serb municipality, and part of the town and Muslim villages were the Muslim municipality, and that the Serb police would not go after criminals in Muslim villages and vice versa? Was that the idea, actually?

utterances.speaker: SRBISLAV DAVIDOVIC
utterances.text: Well, yes, that was the idea, because the very fact that the villages are rather pure ethnically. Perhaps the town itself was a bit more of a problem. But the Muslim police would do its work in Muslim villages, and the Serb police would do their work in Serb villages, and there would be schools for Muslims and Serbs separately. Then also the health centre would be divided. There would be part of the health centre that would treat Serb patients, and another part would treat Muslim patients. Then the government would be divided, companies would be divided up. Some would belong to the Muslims, others would belong to the Serbs. Well, as I've told you, I did not find that very clear. I was quite skeptical about that and about the possibility of that kind of thing functioning, but anyway, that was a political decision made at the time, and we can see what that brought about.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Thank you. Am I right if I say that the city infrastructure, the public utilities, the waterworks, electricity and so on, that would remain as joint companies, and things that could be done at municipal level would be done at municipal level, whereas the town, the city itself, would be one?

utterances.speaker: SRBISLAV DAVIDOVIC
utterances.text: Well, you cannot really build your own waterworks that quickly. You cannot really have a Muslim waterworks and the Serb waterworks, electricity, too. Now, whether that would happen in the future or not, only time could tell. But that did not happen. However, it is certain that at least in the beginning, the infrastructure would be shared, water, electricity, et cetera.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Thank you. Do you agree that the Serb side was a bit more in favour of this idea than the Muslim side but that the Muslim side did accept that too?

utterances.speaker: SRBISLAV DAVIDOVIC
utterances.text: Now -- well, who advocated this to a greater degree? Well, it is possible that it was the Serb side. A bit more.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Do we agree that what the Serbs advocated was remaining in Yugoslavia, however, when that proved to be impossible, then this turned out to be their choice?

utterances.speaker: SRBISLAV DAVIDOVIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Now, I would like to ask you the following: Had Bosnia been reorganised that were -- let's just take the example of Bratunac. Had Bratunac been reorganised this way, would this plan, based on the existence of two municipalities, would that mean that Muslims would be expelled, cleansed from Bratunac, or would they get the same that the Serbs and all the rest would get there?

utterances.speaker: SRBISLAV DAVIDOVIC
utterances.text: Well, it is certain that that plan did not mean any kind of ethnic cleansing on either side. It was in favour of co-existence. How do I call it? Well, yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Co-existence. Yes. Yes. I was wondering how it was interpreted. Yes, well put. Yes. Co-existing. One municipality by the other one.

utterances.speaker: SRBISLAV DAVIDOVIC
utterances.text: Well, yes. No one would prevent the population from mingling. In companies, Serbs and Muslims would go on working together side by side. And then in government, I don't know. Well, it's not that -- I mean, there would be communication. Nobody could stop communication. I mean, it couldn't have been stopped even during the war let alone in peace and given that kind of co-existence.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Thank you. Tell me, at that point in time, did you ever notice in institutions or among prominent individuals any kind of wish to have Muslims expelled or, heaven forbid, killed?

utterances.speaker: SRBISLAV DAVIDOVIC
utterances.text: I told you, no one ever advocated that, and people did not leave Bratunac before the 17th of April, until these paramilitaries appeared and until conflicts started in the neighbouring municipalities. First in the municipality of Bijeljina, and then a number of people started leaving, and then the conflict in Zvornik, and then a bit more people, I mean the Muslim population, started leaving. And then finally when the paramilitaries arrived, then even more Muslim people started leaving Bratunac.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Thank you. At that point in time were there cases of Serb families leaving Bratunac even before the conflict broke out?

utterances.speaker: SRBISLAV DAVIDOVIC
utterances.text: Well, yes. Everyone seemed to feel that things were not moving in the right direction. So even Serbs who had some place to go, say in Serbia, to send their children there, that's what they did, because it was obvious that things were not moving in the right direction. So quite a few Serb women and children left Bratunac too.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: As the conflict was getting closer to Bratunac, it was less because of what was happening in Bratunac itself and more because of everything that was happening throughout Bosnia; right?

utterances.speaker: SRBISLAV DAVIDOVIC
utterances.text: Yes. I've already mentioned Bijeljina, and even more than that, other places that are close to Bratunac.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Thank you. However, in Bratunac itself, I mean not in the town itself but in the villages, in the municipalities, there were extremists on both sides; right?

utterances.speaker: SRBISLAV DAVIDOVIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Did you know anything about the military organisation of the SDA, not to say the Muslims, because not all the Muslims were part of the SDA, so the military organisation of the SDA, of the Patriotic League, and the Green Berets?

utterances.speaker: SRBISLAV DAVIDOVIC
utterances.text: Well, yes. People did talk. Green Berets were being organised in the villages, this Patriotic League. Also, there was guard duty along roads, in front of houses, et cetera. Then it started on the other side too. Serbs guarded their own houses. Muslims guarded their own houses.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Thank you. At one point in time, even in town, in front of apartment buildings there were mixed guards sometimes as well; right?

utterances.speaker: SRBISLAV DAVIDOVIC
utterances.text: Well, yes. Attempts were made to that effect where both Serbs and Muslims lived to have these joint guards, and perhaps in some residential areas where there were privately owned houses, but that happened to a lesser degree. In most cases it was Serbs who were guarding their own and Muslims who were guarding their own.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Thank you. Now, was it correct that Glogova was well known as, not to call it a stronghold, but a location, a place where there were quite a few extremists, and it was being said that there were lists of Serbs that were supposed to be liquidated and that plans were made because of that.

utterances.speaker: SRBISLAV DAVIDOVIC
utterances.text: Well, let me tell you, there were all sorts of rumours that were heard. That's what the Serbs heard, and I assume that the Muslims heard rumours that were the opposite, and I think that this was mutual intimidation. But there were rumours to that effect, yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Thank you. In the Muslim documentation that we are going to deal with later, we'll tender that through another witness, there is something that I'd like to ask you about. Did you hear about March and Potocari, that JNA reservists were attacked and the JNA as such?

utterances.speaker: SRBISLAV DAVIDOVIC
utterances.text: I cannot remember the dates, but it is certain that people talked. There was an incident in this village and in that village, and there was an incident on the road here and there. There were these incidents in the spring months of 1992.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: SRBISLAV DAVIDOVIC
utterances.text: And the beginning.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Thank you. Now, I would just like to enumerate the things that happened, the incidents that occurred before the 17th of April so that we can see what preceded the arrival of these paramilitaries. So here it goes: On the 21st of March in Potocari, three attacks; on the 24th of March, an attack against Buljim; on the 25th of March, incidents in Orahovac, Bukova Glava, at the expulsion of Chetniks, they say, from Bukova Glava; then, on the 25th of March also Bukova Glava, the expulsion of Chetniks; on the 25th of March sabotage in Zeleni Jadar, about ten Chetniks were killed. Have you heard of any of this? I beg your pardon. I really should slow down. There was this sabotage in Zeleni Jadar when ten Chetniks were killed, they say. Were these the workers at the mine in Zeleni Jadar?

utterances.speaker: SRBISLAV DAVIDOVIC
utterances.text: They worked for the forestry industry there. There is a furniture factory there, and there are people who work in the forest itself.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: And then in Nova Kasaba, this --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Please take a look at the previous question and answer. You read out all these -- I wonder whether that's a statement of yours or a question. You read out various places and asked a simple question in relation to the last place. Then the witness answered only in relation to Zeleni Jadar. What purpose would it serve at all? And I'm struggling to understand all these, but make -- ask one question at a time.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you, Excellency. I wanted to summarise this and to hear the witness and to see what he did hear of and what he did not hear of, but I seem to be spending more time this way, and I do apologise for that.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Did you hear about what happened at the JNA warehouse in Nova Kasaba?

utterances.speaker: SRBISLAV DAVIDOVIC
utterances.text: All of these things that you mentioned, it's only Bukova Glava that is in the territory of the municipality of Bratunac. As for some of these things, I did hear about it because it is nearby, after all. The municipality of Srebrenica is very close to us. However, now for me to say with any certainty I did hear this and I didn't hear that, well --

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Ah-ha. What about Konjevic Polje, is that in Bratunac?

utterances.speaker: SRBISLAV DAVIDOVIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Do you remember on the 15th of April they launched some kind of attack and there were no Serbs left in Konjevic Polje?

utterances.speaker: SRBISLAV DAVIDOVIC
utterances.text: There weren't any Serbs in Konjevic Polje anyway. However, there was this road going through Konjevic Polje. The Milici-Zvornik road went through Konjevic Polje, and I think it's on this road they stopped Serbs and there were these incidents where the Serbs were victims.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Thank you do you remember that they attacked a convoy of trucks transporting ore from a mine and that they killed and took prisoner -- took some people prisoner?

utterances.speaker: SRBISLAV DAVIDOVIC
utterances.text: They were taking alumina to Zvornik and there was this incident. And I think that the driver was killed, in actual fact.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Thank you. Can you tell us something about Judge Goran Zekic, who he was, and is it correct that he was killed on the 8th of May in some ambush?

utterances.speaker: SRBISLAV DAVIDOVIC
utterances.text: Goran Zekic had a degree in law. He was a judge in the Municipal Court in Srebrenica. He was the president of the Serb Democratic Party for Srebrenica, and he was a member of parliament. On the 8th of May, he was killed in an ambush.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Thank you. He was a member of the joint Assembly, wasn't he?

utterances.speaker: SRBISLAV DAVIDOVIC
utterances.text: Yes, the joint Assembly.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: How did this affect the general feeling in Bratunac?

utterances.speaker: SRBISLAV DAVIDOVIC
utterances.text: Well, along with Miroslav Deronjic, he was the most important person in the area. What Miroslav was in Bratunac, Zekic was in Srebrenica. And it's nearby. It's 10 kilometres away. So these two were the two most important Serbs in the area, and the connotation was highly negative as far as the Serbs were concerned, both in Srebrenica and in Bratunac.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Thank you. Is it correct that on the 9th of May, a day later, there was an attempt to disarm the people of Glogova and that this was carried out by the JNA, part of the Novi Sad Corps, the Territorial Defence, and the police?

utterances.speaker: SRBISLAV DAVIDOVIC
utterances.text: I think that this was a response to Goran's killing, this operation of disarming Glogova on the 9th of May.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Thank you. You do remember, don't you, that on the 3rd or 4th of May, in Hranca at the entrance into Bratunac, a JNA column was attacked? They were returning to Serbia to Central Bosnia.

utterances.speaker: SRBISLAV DAVIDOVIC
utterances.text: Yes. The JNA was leaving Central Bosnia and other parts of Bosnia, going to Serbia, so they went via Bratunac, and that's where the column was attacked.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Thank you. So there were certain incidents, some before the 17th of April and others after the 17th of April. And the culmination was, isn't that right, on the 8th and 9th of May?

utterances.speaker: SRBISLAV DAVIDOVIC
utterances.text: Yes. The killing of Goran Zekic and the disarming of Glogova.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Thank you. Now, just briefly, these paramilitaries, at first did they introduce themselves as reservists, and then did some of them turn into renegades? And after that, were some of them placed under the command of the Serb army, and were others expelled? Can you tell us briefly what happened.

utterances.speaker: SRBISLAV DAVIDOVIC
utterances.text: No one thought that they were part of the army, no one. Let me deal with this very briefly. These were people who came from Serbia, who had been at the front in Croatia and -- I don't know. Now, what did they look like to us? They wanted to loot. I mean there's one thing I haven't said. Among these volunteers, there were these two women as well. One was called Dragana, and allegedly some Muslims who were training there with the ZNGs had raped them, and it was said that they had come there to take their revenge, and people said that they had found those two men who had done that. However, none of those volunteers got out of Bratunac alive. All of them were killed. They paid with their own lives.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Thank you. So at least two of those killed Muslims were the victims of revenge for the rapes they committed in Croatia while in training there with the ZNG; correct?

utterances.speaker: SRBISLAV DAVIDOVIC
utterances.text: That's what the story was. We thought it was a normal thing to see men there, but we were surprised to see two women as paramilitaries, and then people said that the reason why they joined the paramilitary formations was that they came to find those who had raped them in Croatia.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Thank you. We heard here from some Muslim witnesses that the local Serbs, prominent men and people from the government, told the Muslims to lie low and to stay at home and be patient until the authorities were able to get rid of the paramilitary formations. Do you have any personal knowledge as to that question?

utterances.speaker: SRBISLAV DAVIDOVIC
utterances.text: Well, you see, those paramilitary formations did not make me feel safe either. I was afraid too. I did not suggest to the Muslims to take shelter, although it seemed to have been the right thing to do. I say that, because whoever tried to help anyone else with the best of intentions, it seemed like shooting yourself in the foot, because it turned out to be a good thing for either the Muslims or yourself. Such was the situation. No one could help anyone else. Perhaps they could, but at the risk of their own lives.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Can you explain the situation -- the situations you experienced which would clearly indicate that both Serbs and Muslims feared such groups? Did you have any such incidents where you tried to save some Muslims?

utterances.speaker: SRBISLAV DAVIDOVIC
utterances.text: I wanted to help a good friend of mine, a co-worker by the name of Resid Sinanovic. I tried to help him by asking Miroslav Deronjic, on Resid's request, to provide passes for Resid and his family since they wanted to leave Bratunac and join his brother in Skopje, who was a JNA captain. He told him that the situation to him did not look like something that would get any better and wanted to get away. It was on the 5th of May. I remember it, because my saint patron's day was on the 6th. I tried to explain it to Miroslav. The next day, in the morning, Miroslav provided me with four clean passes, and he said, You fill them out. I went to Resid's apartment, and there was his wife, his two sons, and he. We filled in the clean passes, we bid farewell, and he told me he was supposed to go to Bjelovac where his parents lived. It was around 12.00 on the 6th. He was going to decide whether to continue immediately or to leave for Skopje the next day. He didn't have a very reliable car at the time. He had a Fico, F-i-c-o. So he decided in the end to leave in the morning, on the 7th. Later on, he retold his story for me. He crossed a bridge at Ljubovija, some 3 kilometres from Bratunac across the Drina. He entered Serbia in Ljubovija next to a motel which is 3 kilometres from the bridge. The Ljubovija police awaited him, stopped him and returned him to Bratunac. They took him back across the bridge. And from Bratunac, he went to Bjelovac, and then across the hills he took his wife and kids to safety, to Zenica.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: In other words, Deronjic's passes did not amount to much across the river.

utterances.speaker: SRBISLAV DAVIDOVIC
utterances.text: No, not in Serbia, although I don't know why. Our police did let him pass through across the bridge with the passes he had though. The policeman knew him, too. He had been a chief of police in a pre-war period. So our policeman let him go, but the Ljubovija policeman made him go back.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Thank you. You also had some experience with your family and relatives. They, too, tried to help some others.

utterances.speaker: SRBISLAV DAVIDOVIC
utterances.text: Well, we had all lived there for years. We are neighbours, and everyone was trying to help everyone else. However, there were many cases when people tried to help and yet it would have been better that they had not, because later on those who were helped were killed.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Thank you. Is it correct that by that time the rumour had it that each Muslim had a Serb to kill, whereas you, in the town itself, were trying to help each other?

utterances.speaker: SRBISLAV DAVIDOVIC
utterances.text: Well, there were lots of stories going around, all sorts of things on both sides.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Thank you. Is it correct that at the time, in May, the Muslims around Bratunac -- not in Bratunac itself but surrounding Bratunac, put up barricades which resulted in Bratunac being completely cut off from the rest of Bosnia-Herzegovina and Republika Srpska?

utterances.speaker: SRBISLAV DAVIDOVIC
utterances.text: The Muslims had left Bratunac. As for the roads, Bratunac could only communicate with Serbia, because in the direction of Konjevic Polje there were Muslims. There was a Muslim village there along the road. So for a while, Bratunac only had one road open to Serbia.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Thank you. Is it correct that in early May you received some 5.000 Serbs who had fled Srebrenica and that by that time the Serbs from Zenica and Central Bosnia began arriving too?

utterances.speaker: SRBISLAV DAVIDOVIC
utterances.text: Yes. Bratunac took in all the Srebrenica Serbs. I think some 5.000 of them arrived from the municipality of Srebrenica. At the same time, Serbs from some Central Bosnia municipalities arrived, as well as some people from Zenica, et cetera. Bratunac must have taken in some 6- to 7.000 refugees at the time.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Thank you. Before that, on the 1st or 2nd of May, Gojko Stjepanovic was killed in Bljeceva. And on the 8th of May, Zekic was killed. It became obvious that it would be very difficult to avoid having a war.

utterances.speaker: SRBISLAV DAVIDOVIC
utterances.text: The first victim on the Serb side was Gojko Jovanovic from Bljeceva as well as Milo Zekic and his wife. They were the first victims, and it all took place around the 1st or 2nd of May. They were the Serb -- first Serb victims in 1992.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Thank you. Is it correct that at the time the municipal authorities had no power whatsoever to deal with the paramilitary formations and that the paramilitaries even slapped prominent people around and took some of them parading through town while they were tied up?

utterances.speaker: SRBISLAV DAVIDOVIC
utterances.text: Well, yes. The -- I tried to explain that the paramilitary formation was as much of a problem for the Muslims as it was for the Serbs, and I speak strictly from my point of view. No one could hold any sway over them. They were armed. They had vehicles. They just kept driving around along the roads, and we thought that they were going to wage the whole war by driving around, judging by their behaviour.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Who was the most prominent person in the police on the Serb side, and was he trying to stand up to them?

utterances.speaker: SRBISLAV DAVIDOVIC
utterances.text: The commander of the Bratunac police at the time was Milutin Milosevic. In my view, as I knew him, he was the only person who intended to stand up to them, but unfortunately, in Sandici village, just beyond Kravica, he was killed in an ambush alongside another 11 Serbs. I think he was the only person who meant to deal with the paramilitary formations seriously. To his misfortune and ours, he was killed early on.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: So it was an ambush in Sandici in 1992, at the very beginning, where he and another 11 Serbs were killed.

utterances.speaker: SRBISLAV DAVIDOVIC
utterances.text: Yes. I think so.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Following the paramilitary formations -- let -- tell us first, how did it come that they were killed, for the most part?

utterances.speaker: SRBISLAV DAVIDOVIC
utterances.text: Well, they kept driving along the road between Srebrenica and Bratunac. On one occasion, the Muslims set up an ambush in Potocari and killed four. Then if -- as one goes on to Glogova and Kravica, they were all killed in their cars.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Thank you. Following that -- sorry. Before that there was this Makedonac person, and then there was someone else from Montenegro.

utterances.speaker: SRBISLAV DAVIDOVIC
utterances.text: There were different kinds of paramilitary formations. There was this Bosanac person and then a Bekija and others. I no longer remember who and what they were.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Thank you. Is it correct that even Deronjic was beaten up as well as other prominent Serbs?

utterances.speaker: SRBISLAV DAVIDOVIC
utterances.text: Yes, there were. I can tell you of more prominent people from Bratunac who were beaten up or mistreated by them.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: If one wanted to help a Muslim, you had to ask him not to tell anyone. Otherwise, you would be hurt too; correct?

utterances.speaker: SRBISLAV DAVIDOVIC
utterances.text: It's difficult to talk about that. You were not supposed to even think or mention helping a Muslim, let alone do.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Do you recall that Deronjic asked us and even visited us when we were in Zvornik -- he was basically asking for help to deal with the renegades in his municipality?

utterances.speaker: SRBISLAV DAVIDOVIC
utterances.text: I talked to Deronjic frequently. We were next-door neighbours, and I told him, Deronjic, well, you need to put a stop to this. What is this paramilitary presence? His late father was saying the same thing. He was trying to tell him to tackle it. Some Muslims came to see his father as well. Many people knew his father. Since World War II, he was the co-operative manager, and he hailed from the village of Magasici, which is adjacent to the village of Glogova. Many Muslims came to Miroslav's father, Milan, trying to ask him to use his influence over his son to put a stop to these paramilitary formations. It's difficult to describe these situations. Those paramilitary formations were not dear to my heart, and I can only imagine how the Muslims felt.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Is it true that the they also beat up the brigade commander and that Mauzer had a clash with them because they had taken one of his soldiers prisoner and he turned his APCs on them?

utterances.speaker: SRBISLAV DAVIDOVIC
utterances.text: That was the conflict with Mijovic. He was sent from Serbia. He was sent from the Serbian DB, and he kept bringing in prominent Serbs, beating them up. He took Obrenovic in, who at the time must have been over 50. He beat him up. Then there was Dragan Trisic, who was later on assistant commander for logistics. He refused to provide him with fuel, and then he beat him up. And then Pavle Loncarevic, who was a company director, was also beaten up. Then Zoran Radic and many other prominent men. They were all beaten up by Mijovic and his paramilitary soldiers.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: One other question before the break. Is it correct that the local authorities were sealing off the apartments left by Muslims so that they be preserved until they returned and then you received the 7- or 8.000 refugees?

utterances.speaker: SRBISLAV DAVIDOVIC
utterances.text: Yes, that was the attempt they made at the outset, but when this stampede of Srebrenica refugees came upon us, things were no longer under control. People went into empty Muslim houses on their own.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you. I am looking at the clocks, Your Excellencies. Can I keep on, or are we going on a break so that I can move on to the next topic when we return?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: We are going to have a break and resume at 11.00.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Yes, Mr. Harvey.

utterances.speaker: MR. HARVEY
utterances.text: Your Honours, if I may, please, introduce to the court Ms. Tatiana - I knew I'd get this wrong - Jancarkova, who has been a pro bono legal assistant with my team for many months but who we will sadly be losing soon. She has been a terrific assistance because of her B/C/S expertise, in particular, and her legal acumen. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Thank you. Yes, Mr. Karadzic.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you, Your Excellency.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Mr. Davidovic, I will now try to get to the events of 1995 as soon as possible, so I will try to formulate the remaining questions from the other period in such a way that you can answer with just a yes or no, but whenever you feel you need to expand upon that, please feel free to do so. Is it true that in early April, before the arrival of these warriors in their cars from Serbia and Croatia, the Green Berets also displayed their presence in the street and checked vehicles and -- and passengers?

utterances.speaker: SRBISLAV DAVIDOVIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: So that was yes.

utterances.speaker: SRBISLAV DAVIDOVIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Thank you. Is it correct that Glogova had about 2.000 inhabitants and that after this disarming operation between 50 to 60 people were killed, but you don't know how that happened.

utterances.speaker: SRBISLAV DAVIDOVIC
utterances.text: I know that 60 people were killed, but I don't know the details.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Thank you. Is it correct that in December 1992, in a village called Bjelovac, which was predominantly Serb, 109 Serb civilians were killed?

utterances.speaker: SRBISLAV DAVIDOVIC
utterances.text: Yes, in a single day.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Before that, 35 people were killed near Bratunac; correct?

utterances.speaker: SRBISLAV DAVIDOVIC
utterances.text: In that same village in Bjelovac.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Thank you. Is it true that in our earlier political system each municipality had a Territorial Defence brigade and the president of the municipality was ex officio the president of the Defence council and the civilian commander, as it were, of such brigade?

utterances.speaker: SRBISLAV DAVIDOVIC
utterances.text: It is true that each municipality had its own Territorial Defence. However, whether that unit was at the brigade level or not, I don't know, and I don't know about the president of the municipality being the commander of such a unit, but in short, they did have their Territorial Defence units.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Thank you. Now, is it true that the Territorial Defence had also stored within various companies and factories arms and weapons that belonged to it?

utterances.speaker: SRBISLAV DAVIDOVIC
utterances.text: Yes, that's true. They had their own depots there including weapons, equipment, and uniforms.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Thank you. Is it correct that the president of the municipal board, in other words, of the local government ex officio was the head of the civilian protection service?

utterances.speaker: SRBISLAV DAVIDOVIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Thank you. Is it correct that these municipal Territorial Defence units later became municipal brigades, that they kept their municipal titles or names and that the municipality funded these units and provided logistics for them?

utterances.speaker: SRBISLAV DAVIDOVIC
utterances.text: Yes. I don't know when the Territorial Defence actually turned into a military formation and when it was renamed to become the Bratunac Brigade. And what was -- what else was it that you asked me?

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: That the municipality --

utterances.speaker: SRBISLAV DAVIDOVIC
utterances.text: Yes, logistics. Yes, the logistics for the brigade was provided by and funded by the municipality, which means that they provided for their food, uniforms or clothing, cigarettes and so on, depending on what they could afford, depending on the economy, the local economy.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Thank you. Am I correct when I explained to the Main Staff during the war that the municipalities would actually provide more funds for their own municipal units, for their own children, as it were, than they would for the central Main Staff?

utterances.speaker: SRBISLAV DAVIDOVIC
utterances.text: I believe that you were right in that.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Thank you. Do you agree that the so-called Crisis Staffs, for instance, right now during this freeze, they still exist, that these Crisis Staffs were not a new body? They were just had to be organised for novel conditions, and they were not a new form of government, as it were?

utterances.speaker: SRBISLAV DAVIDOVIC
utterances.text: Well, I believe that Crisis Staffs comprise the existing officials, the president of the municipality, the defence ministry, the civilian protection, and so on. So they were members of those Crisis Staffs ex officio, and that's how it was at the beginning.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Thank you. So would you agree that these Crisis Staffs were set up so that procedures and dead-lines and delays would be avoided? In other words, they focused on their work, and if they were members of the Crisis Staff, there were no dead-lines or anything. They had to report immediately.

utterances.speaker: SRBISLAV DAVIDOVIC
utterances.text: Well, yes. They had to in order to be operational.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Thank you. Do you agree with me that even today, there is a lot of snow there right now, Crisis Staffs are still in existence and in operation?

utterances.speaker: SRBISLAV DAVIDOVIC
utterances.text: Well, yes, throughout Serbia. Well, nowadays they call them staffs for -- staffs for natural disasters, but the purpose is the same.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Thank you. Now I would like to move to 1994. In 1994, you were invited as a professional, although you were a member of an opposition party, you were invited to take control or to be -- to head the municipal authorities.

utterances.speaker: SRBISLAV DAVIDOVIC
utterances.text: Well, the post of president of the Executive Committee is appointed by the Assembly. I actually was there as a candidate. There was another candidate, and I won.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: The Assembly had a majority of SDS seats; correct?

utterances.speaker: SRBISLAV DAVIDOVIC
utterances.text: Well, yes, probably, but not absolute -- probably an absolute majority.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Thank you. Do you remember that I, as well as other members of the SDS during the war, insisted on confidence votes when needed, and at one point in time the chief of police actually was removed from his post, although he hadn't done anything wrong, but he was not successful in preventing looting and things like that? So do you recall that at that time the municipal government, too, was replaced? There was a reshuffle there too.

utterances.speaker: SRBISLAV DAVIDOVIC
utterances.text: Well, in the course of the war, the municipal authorities performed their functions in keeping with the law. That includes the president of the Executive Council, the police commander and others. And of course if someone failed to perform properly or competently in their position, they would be replaced.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Thank you. Did you learn that some actions were taken around Srebrenica before the operation or did you, yourself, see that some soldiers appeared on the perimeters of the protected area?

utterances.speaker: SRBISLAV DAVIDOVIC
utterances.text: Are you referring to 1995?

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: SRBISLAV DAVIDOVIC
utterances.text: Well, let me put it this way: People knew about this operation. I mean, people who were in the army talked about it. They knew about it, of course. And of course everyone had family members, and that's how word spread. So everyone more or less knew that they would move on Srebrenica in order to separate the enclaves, to cut them off.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: [No interpretation]

utterances.speaker: SRBISLAV DAVIDOVIC
utterances.text: Well, yes, that there would be an operation in order to separate the enclaves of Srebrenica and Zepa in order to contain them -- or, rather, so that there could be more control over the enclaves, because these enclaves were used to launch various sabotage actions by Muslims against civilians, and in order to put that under control, the operation was launched on Srebrenica.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Slow down, Mr. Karadzic. So separating the enclaves, cutting them off was part of your question, not part of the answer. Please do not overlap or put a pause between the questions and answers. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: I would like this to be translated to the witness.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: You heard, Mr. Davidovic. Please put a pause before you start answering the question, for the benefit of the interpreters.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I will do my best.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Yes, Mr. Karadzic.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] With all due respect, the witness was the first to mention the separation of enclaves, and that was in the last lines of page 40, and then I asked whether that was the purpose of this.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Now, do you agree with me that the agreement envisaged that the Zeleni Jadar-Podravanje-Skelani road between the enclaves was under this agreement ours and that it was cut off because of this unlawful expansion of the enclaves?

utterances.speaker: SRBISLAV DAVIDOVIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Thank you. At one point when these actions began -- or, rather, do you agree with me that this is precisely where these actions began, between the enclaves Zeleni Jadar and so on; in other words, to the south of the -- Srebrenica?

utterances.speaker: SRBISLAV DAVIDOVIC
utterances.text: Well, yes. To the north, it was Serbia and Bratunac. It was territory controlled by Serbs. And on the southern side, that's where the Muslim enclaves were. And this in reference to Bratunac.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Thank you. You mentioned actions launched from Srebrenica. Did you know of the existence of the 28th Division, earlier known as the 8th Operational Group? Did you know who their commander was, and were you aware of their frequent raids or actions into the Serb territories?

utterances.speaker: SRBISLAV DAVIDOVIC
utterances.text: Well, yes, I did know. People knew about the existence, and they -- their existence, and it numbered about 7.000 men, and it was under the command of Naser Oric.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Did tragedies follow once they left the enclaves and ventured into Serb villages, and who were the victims usually in those villages?

utterances.speaker: SRBISLAV DAVIDOVIC
utterances.text: Well, they left the enclaves on several occasions to attack Serb villages, and mostly in these villages it was the civilian population that they attacked.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Thank you. Do you remember any particular such action?

utterances.speaker: SRBISLAV DAVIDOVIC
utterances.text: Well, there were a number of those, but I remember an action at Christmas time on Kravica in 1993, and then there was another one in Fakovici, in Skelani. All these were raids launched from the enclaves where there would be anywhere between 20 and 60 victims each time. There were a number of such raids on Serb villages launched from these enclaves.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Is it correct that they did not spare women or children or even cattle? If they couldn't take it with them, they would just kill them?

utterances.speaker: SRBISLAV DAVIDOVIC
utterances.text: Well, there were all kinds of horrors there. There was murder, there was torching of houses, looting, and all the worst.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Is it true that there is a big cemetery where these victims were -- their victims were buried and that there were women and children who were buried there, all these victims of Oric's units?

utterances.speaker: SRBISLAV DAVIDOVIC
utterances.text: Well, most of the people from the Srebrenica and Bratunac municipality were buried in that cemetery, because Srebrenica was captured, and the largest part of the Bratunac cemetery now -- or, rather, the -- the size of the Bratunac cemetery is huge, much bigger than would be necessary for a town the size of Bratunac, which numbers about 7.000 inhabitants.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Thank you. Now, you were president of the local government when you went to Pribicevac; correct?

utterances.speaker: SRBISLAV DAVIDOVIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Ms. West mentioned that this was a very unpleasant encounter with Mladic, who did not show much respect for the civilian authorities, and he wanted you to be in the trenches.

utterances.speaker: SRBISLAV DAVIDOVIC
utterances.text: Well, yes. He was very unpleasant, and he treated me with a lot of arrogance, if I can put it that way, although I told him who I was. I told him that I was the president of the Executive Committee of the Bratunac municipality, but he never showed in any way that he knew of me. It was only the next day that he showed that, but that's the kind of person he was. He treated people like that. It wasn't just me that he treated in this manner. He also treated his own men and people in that way.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Do you agree that that was not his personal attitude towards you? That is precisely what I wanted to ask. Rather, our officers were closer to parties of the left than to the SDS.

utterances.speaker: SRBISLAV DAVIDOVIC
utterances.text: Well, I don't know whether he was irritated by that. I was not even wearing a uniform at the time. I arrived there wearing civilian clothes. Maybe that irritated him too. What I was doing there in civilian clothes when there's a war going on.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Thank you. However, do you assume that he thought that you were a member of the SDS since you were in government? Do you agree that our army was closer to the parties of the left?

utterances.speaker: SRBISLAV DAVIDOVIC
utterances.text: Yes, yes. Now, whether he thought that I was a member of the SDS, well, perhaps people found that a bit strange then. I was not part of that political option, and I held a particular office. So maybe that was his assumption too.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Thank you. It was your understanding -- or, actually, did you know that their army had withdrawn from Srebrenica and that our army entered that town without any kind of serious resistance?

utterances.speaker: SRBISLAV DAVIDOVIC
utterances.text: Well, there was some small resistance, but not the kind of resistance that we had all expected. It was only on the following day that I understood that the army had withdrawn to other places, or, rather, that they were not defending Srebrenica.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: [Microphone not activated]

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: Microphone, please.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Mr. Karadzic, microphone.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I beg your pardon.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: In this conversation that was recorded on the 25th of February, 1998, and also in other statements, you said that you found out -- actually, you said in this interview 15- to 16.000, and then later on up to 20.000 civilians flowed into Potocari, Muslim civilians arrived in Potocari; is that right?

utterances.speaker: SRBISLAV DAVIDOVIC
utterances.text: Well, that is my rough estimate. It was hard to give any kind of accurate estimate. It's masses of people at a particular place. Now, was it 16.000? Was it 20.000? One thing is for sure, there were lots of people there. It's certainly not an exaggerated figure. Perhaps the figure I gave was even smaller than what happened in real life.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Thank you. And you came there as a representative of the municipal authorities to see whether the soldiers needed anything. This had to do with what was happening in Srebrenica; right?

utterances.speaker: SRBISLAV DAVIDOVIC
utterances.text: Well, the brigade was asking for a lot, and that was unusual. Food, civilians, uniforms, boots, and so on. And I went up there to this Pribicevac where there was this one battalion. It was the 3rd Battalion. Their location was the most difficult of all, and I wanted to see what the situation was regarding food, cigarettes, et cetera.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: So you were there in your official capacity, just as you had been informed in your official capacity that there were civilians, many civilians, in Potocari, and that the sick should be taken care of as well. And as you said in your interview, people were milling about, and they were supposed to be supplied with food and water. Can you tell us what you did there, you the authorities?

utterances.speaker: SRBISLAV DAVIDOVIC
utterances.text: At the meeting at the Fontana Hotel on the 12th, we were given a specific task -- or, rather, when it became clear that the Muslims from Srebrenica did not wish to remain in the area. It was when they officially stated that they wanted to leave the area. Then General Mladic said to us, You gentlemen from the civilian structures, make an effort now to the best of your ability to help that civilian population in Potocari in terms of logistics supplies, water supplies, food supplies, health care. The meeting was almost over. Say it was between 11.00 and 11.30. Then I and the president of the municipality, Simic, went to the municipality, and we worked out a plan as to what we should do to help the population in Potocari. For that purpose, we mobilised two water trucks, one from the public utilities company and the other one from the fire brigade. All the bread that was baked by our bakery was supposed to be sent up there. In the Red Cross we found some food, some cookies, I believe. All of that was supposed to be sent up there too. However, we thought that all of that was not enough, so in the neighbouring Republic of Serbia we asked the municipality of Ljubovija, that is 6 kilometres away from Bratunac, we asked for help so that they could give us whatever they could afford. So they sent us bread, a water truck. And then the municipality of Zvornik too. President Simic was also supposed to contact the UNHCR, because he had already had communication with them. So they were supposed to take part in this action too.
