Already two hours after the end of the meeting we were in Potocari along with these supplies, and we distributed that to the people up there, although up there the delegation that attended the meeting in the Fontana Hotel was not there. Mandic, the president of the municipality, then Ibro, and a woman named Camila, they were supposed to meet us up there once we arrived with this humanitarian aid, and then they were supposed to distribute it. However, they did not meet us there, so we were doing this as best we could spontaneously, if I can put it that way. They could have probably done this in the right kind of order had they met us there. They would have known, but anyway. We tried to help the population up there to the best of our ability. Truth to tell, our help was not sufficient, I'm sure of that, but we tried to send even more than we could actually afford, but that certainly was not sufficient, because there were lots of people up there.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Thank you. Now, I would like to ask you to specify something. I'd like to see whether I understood you correctly. Did you know that on the evening of the 11th there were two meeting at the Fontana Hotel, but you did not attend them; right?

utterances.speaker: SRBISLAV DAVIDOVIC
utterances.text: That's right. That's correct. It was only at this meeting on the 12th at 10.00 I realised that that meeting had been preceded by another meeting which was attended only by Nesib Mandic, the president of the municipality. That was on the 11th, in the evening, I think. I don't know. And then he could not say what it was that the people wanted, but he agreed, probably with General Mladic, that he would go to Srebrenica and that he would come on the following day with the definite view as to what it was that they wanted. That was my understanding at the meeting, that this was their final position, that they wanted to leave the area of Srebrenica.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Thank you. Let me try to work this out now. There was one meeting with Karremans. There was the second meeting with Karremans and the Muslims on the 11th. Up until then, people did not know whether the civilians would return home or whether they would stand by the decision to leave the area, and that was defined at the meeting that you attended on the 12th at 10.00 in Fontana; right?

utterances.speaker: SRBISLAV DAVIDOVIC
utterances.text: That's right.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Am I right if I say that up until then it was uncertain whether they would leave, and until then buses had not been mobilised, and no one realised that they would leave for sure.

utterances.speaker: SRBISLAV DAVIDOVIC
utterances.text: I did not know that that would happen.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Thank you. So you were there personally in Potocari when this food was being distributed; right?

utterances.speaker: SRBISLAV DAVIDOVIC
utterances.text: Well, in this first convoy that we brought, the water truck, the bread, et cetera.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Thank you. Can you tell us who was present at the meeting on the 12th?

utterances.speaker: SRBISLAV DAVIDOVIC
utterances.text: At the hotel. That meeting was attended by General Mladic, General Krstic, the commander of the Dutch Battalion, his deputy, the interpreter, the delegation of the Muslims consisting of Nesib Mandic, the President of the municipality, and Ibro Nuhanovic [Realtime transcript read in error "Pavlovic"] and Camila from the civilian authorities of Bratunac. There was Ljubisav Simic, the president of the Municipal Assembly; Miroslav Deronjic; and I. The chief of the security centre from Zvornik, Vasic, was present there as well, and there was an officer. I think he was a colonel of the Army of Republika Srpska. That were the attendees at that meeting.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Thank you. What was Mladic's position? I believe that he was the only one who spoke. What was Mladic's position? Were the Muslims expected to express their views or was something imposed on them?

utterances.speaker: SRBISLAV DAVIDOVIC
utterances.text: The meeting was chaired by General Mladic, and he asked, What is your decision? His offer to them was that they could stay if they so wished in the areas where they had lived until then, along with all guarantees of freedom of movement as enjoyed by the rest of the population, the non-Muslims. However, the Muslims would have to hand over their weapons while those who had bloodied their hands would be prosecuted. So all the others could live there safely, enjoying the same rights like the rest of the population, the non-Muslim population. They were very set in their determination to leave the area.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Thank you. As for those first departures in 1992, there was practically 100 per cent certainty that this was temporary and that they would -- they would come back. Was there the possibility of them coming back some day in this case, and did some of them eventually return?

utterances.speaker: SRBISLAV DAVIDOVIC
utterances.text: At the meeting itself that was not discussed. However, now the situation is as follows: Whoever wanted to return, did return. Everybody had their property returned 100 per cent. A lot of houses were repaired and so on. However, on the 12th at that meeting, that was not discussed, whether it was temporary or permanent. If they wanted to leave, they could leave, and there was no mention of whether it was temporary or permanent.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Thank you. When you were in Potocari, did you see a film that shows that day in Potocari, the 12th of July? Did you see a film? Does that film faithfully represent what you saw, that there was no pressure there, no strictness? As you said, people were milling about, and everybody as trying to find a solution for themselves.

utterances.speaker: SRBISLAV DAVIDOVIC
utterances.text: I spent about two hours there. While I was there, I did not see anyone harassing anyone else, beating anyone else, abusing, mistreating anyone else. I said that there were masses of people there. There were also the members of the Dutch Battalion. When we arrived, the Dutch soldiers were lined up. Say it was a line 40 or 50 metres long. And in this way they had cordoned off the people from Srebrenica from the road where the army and police of Republika Srpska were moving, as were others. My understanding was that the role of the soldiers from the Dutch Battalion was to prevent anyone from going to the place where the people were and to prevent people from getting out onto the road. Now -- actually, it's hard for you to imagine what it was like in Potocari. People were milling about there, and there's this river there, but no one could get there from the road.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: You said milling about, and -- let me help the interpreters. And it's not even Pavlovic, it is Ibro Nuhanovic; right?

utterances.speaker: SRBISLAV DAVIDOVIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: All right. Was there any strictness there? Were people just walking around? Did you see that film?

utterances.speaker: SRBISLAV DAVIDOVIC
utterances.text: I saw lots of films. They're shown on TV now as well.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Is it correct that it wasn't -- that people were treated strictly, but they were milling about, as you said very picturesquely?

utterances.speaker: SRBISLAV DAVIDOVIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: You recognised some people?

utterances.speaker: SRBISLAV DAVIDOVIC
utterances.text: Or they recognised me, to put it better.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: So they called out to you and you spoke to them?

utterances.speaker: SRBISLAV DAVIDOVIC
utterances.text: Yes. I spoke with some of them.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: However, there was this real possibility that someone took -- take a personal revenge for the things that had taken place in the three years up to that point?

utterances.speaker: SRBISLAV DAVIDOVIC
utterances.text: Well, in Potocari there were different soldiers there, but I didn't see any Bratunac Brigade members. I simply didn't know the soldiers who were there. And as for the Bratunac Brigade, I know them. The soldiers that were there were people I didn't know. I don't know whether it was a unit from Zvornik or Vlasenica or Milici or some other, perhaps, police unit. In any case, I didn't know the soldiers. There wasn't much possibility of people taking revenge. I also told you there were DutchBat soldiers there as well. And I didn't see anyone trying to mistreat anyone or take revenge.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Thank you. But the area was probably cordoned off -- well, we can see that the people were mingling there and milling about.

utterances.speaker: SRBISLAV DAVIDOVIC
utterances.text: Well, they were supposed to take the people to a larger area where everyone could stay, and then people simply dispersed up to a kilometre away.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Thank you. Is it correct that as the people came in, you tried to keep some order, and you said today that you tried to make an arrangement with the Muslim authorities to wait for you there and help in organising.

utterances.speaker: SRBISLAV DAVIDOVIC
utterances.text: Well, yes. They were more familiar with the people. They knew their priorities. We didn't have enough supplies for everyone. You can just imagine when hungry and thirsty people burst in.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: You had enough water but only limited quantities of bread. You had as much as the bakery could produce and what you received from the municipality of Ljubija in Serbia.

utterances.speaker: SRBISLAV DAVIDOVIC
utterances.text: Well, water was an easy thing to deal with. There was also a river nearby. Food was more difficult.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Thank you. You were also informed that you as the civilian protection were to take care of some 40 or so wounded and sick; correct?

utterances.speaker: SRBISLAV DAVIDOVIC
utterances.text: Yes. In the health centre in Bratunac, we placed some 20 beds. People were accommodated. Some were on the beds and were all medically assisted.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Did you establish that for the occasion, because of the inhabitants who turned up in Potocari?

utterances.speaker: SRBISLAV DAVIDOVIC
utterances.text: Yes. Before that we didn't have beds, because our population went to the hospital in Zvornik. It was only provisionally made for the situation itself.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Is it correct that once the cameras left that someone took the supplies from the people that had been given to them, like chocolate and bread? Did anyone take it away from them?

utterances.speaker: SRBISLAV DAVIDOVIC
utterances.text: It was -- it would be crazy. No one could have done that. Whatever you distributed was gone the same moment. There's no discussion about that.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Thank you. After the third meeting, in the afternoon, on the 12th of July, vehicles began arriving, buses and trucks; right?

utterances.speaker: SRBISLAV DAVIDOVIC
utterances.text: I saw that at around 8.00 p.m. I was in my office in the municipal building. I was there with Dragan Mirkovic, the public utilities company director. All of a sudden we heard from our first-floor window that there was some noise and vehicles arriving. We looked out and saw three buses parking in front of the municipal building.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Before the meeting on the -- the third meeting in the Fontana in the afternoon of the 12th, no one had been evacuated?

utterances.speaker: SRBISLAV DAVIDOVIC
utterances.text: That is correct. In the afternoon on the 12th when the meeting was concluded at around 11.30, that's when means of transport were sought and buses arrived later in the afternoon.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: I would like to clarify something. Were you present during a telephone conversation between myself and Deronjic on the 11th or 13th of July?

utterances.speaker: SRBISLAV DAVIDOVIC
utterances.text: No. I was never present during any conversation between you and Deronjic.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: I'm sorry, then. I must have confused you with another witness. In any case, you heard that on the 11th, Deronjic was appointed civilian affairs commissioner in Srebrenica?

utterances.speaker: SRBISLAV DAVIDOVIC
utterances.text: Yes. Deronjic said so.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Thank you. On the 13th, did you also send water to the Muslims who were captured during their breakthrough attempt, who were then gathered at Sandici meadow?

utterances.speaker: SRBISLAV DAVIDOVIC
utterances.text: No. The buses in front of the municipality - I mentioned three - in front of them there was a policeman when we came out, in front of the first bus. We asked him where these people came from. He said, Well, we brought them in. We asked him where they were going. He replied that they were to go to Batkovic to be exchanged. Then at some point I saw a man on the bus knocking against the window, and I recognised him. I think he was an Omo Jahic from Bljeceva. He worked in the mine and was municipal deputy before the war. I told the policeman that there was a man trying to tell me something, and I asked to be allowed to get in the bus. It was already dark by that time, but still it was very hot and humid. The policeman allowed me in, and I asked him, Omo, what do you want? He used my nickname. He said, Buco, brother, could you provide some water? And I asked the policeman if I could. He said, If you have it, go ahead. There was a water fountain in front of the municipality, and we found a plastic water tank, and when we told them they could get water, they all managed to have one such water tank. We took them all, filled them up with water and gave them to them. We did the same with the other bus, and we filled up at least 50 such water tanks. Perhaps that's what you meant when you asked me about water being provided for the people at Sandici, but I didn't take any water to Sandici.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Could it have been someone else then working for the civilian protection as part of your operation? Did anyone take water trucks to Sandici?

utterances.speaker: SRBISLAV DAVIDOVIC
utterances.text: It is possible, because we had the fire brigade under us, and they had a water truck. It is possible they took water there.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Thank you. Did you hear anything about the incident in Kravica on the 13th of July in the evening, and if so, when?

utterances.speaker: SRBISLAV DAVIDOVIC
utterances.text: I heard about it on the 14th in the morning at 7.00. Two co-operative managers, Jovan Nikolic and Dragan Nikolic arrived in my office. They told me what had happened the previous day in the afternoon in the co-operative at Kravica. It was the first time I heard of it. I was astonished. That's the first time I heard about the event.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Thank you. Please go ahead.

utterances.speaker: SRBISLAV DAVIDOVIC
utterances.text: Well, they stayed with me for an hour or so, told me some details about what happened, and they, too, had problems by the Serb -- caused by the Serb soldiers who did that, who were there. They said that several hundred people were killed in Kravica and that the corpses were still there.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: They were appalled too?

utterances.speaker: SRBISLAV DAVIDOVIC
utterances.text: Yes. They wanted to know what to do, because there wasn't much for them to do anyhow. It was a military operation. If anyone was to do anything, it was the army to do so. There was nothing there for us.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: What did you learn about how the incident took place?

utterances.speaker: SRBISLAV DAVIDOVIC
utterances.text: What I learned was that a Muslim prisoner took a policeman's rifle and killed him. It provoked a reaction, and they were all killed, massacred. Now, whether it was so or not, I don't know. That's the story I heard.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Mr. Davidovic, who did you hear that from?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honour, I can't be certain that it is the two men who told me that, the two Nikolics. In all likelihood they told me that, but I may have heard it later on as well. I no longer know who I heard it from.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Thank you. Yes, Mr. Karadzic.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: But that's the story that prevailed and was taken as true by most. That's the story everyone was familiar with.

utterances.speaker: SRBISLAV DAVIDOVIC
utterances.text: Yes. That is why I am uncertain who told me first. I heard certain variations later on.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Thank you. Following your conversation with the policeman guarding the buses who told you they were to go to Batkovic, did you think that all of the prisoners would be indeed taken there? Did you have any knowledge, or were you under an impression that there were other plans in store for them?

utterances.speaker: SRBISLAV DAVIDOVIC
utterances.text: Well, I was convinced it would be so. Nothing had happened up to that point. At that time, there were 80 captured Serb soldiers from Majevica who were held in Tuzla, and apparently these prisoners were to be exchanged for the soldiers in Tuzla. I was convinced it would turn out that way.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Thank you. You were also under the impression that the incident in Kravica had not been planned but that it was triggered by the killing, when the rifle was taken away from a policeman.

utterances.speaker: SRBISLAV DAVIDOVIC
utterances.text: Well, I was so much surprised that -- I was so astonished, because as I said, at the Fontana meeting, there wasn't even a hint of anything like that. I thought that the things agreed on at the meeting were to be implemented that way. It will never be clear to me how things got out of hand to that extent and why it all happened. The story is that the reason was when the rifle was taken from the policeman and he was killed.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Do you remember that the event in Kravica back in 1993 could have been a further circumstance which made the flaring up of the situation in 1995 easier?

utterances.speaker: SRBISLAV DAVIDOVIC
utterances.text: It's all possible. There was a war, and I really don't know what to think of it. It could have contributed.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: It's difficult to deal with all that misery; right?

utterances.speaker: SRBISLAV DAVIDOVIC
utterances.text: Well, yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Do you know how the bodies were buried? Do you know whether it was done by the municipal services and whether they were in charge of taking hygiene and sanitation measures?

utterances.speaker: SRBISLAV DAVIDOVIC
utterances.text: Well, I wasn't interested. To me, everything that was done was done by the army. They mobilised part of the civilian protection, and it seems they participated in the cleaning up afterwards. However, no one asked me anything about that, and I didn't issue any orders to anyone, including the civilian protection in that regard.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Thank you. Under our law, the army could mobilise the civilian protection.

utterances.speaker: SRBISLAV DAVIDOVIC
utterances.text: Yes. The Ministry of Defence had that right. The civilian protection was under their cap, and they could assign them as they wished.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Thank you. Did you know anything about the requests of certain officers to accommodate some soldiers, to billet them there, and how Deronjic and the civilian authorities resist that attempt asking that they be taken out of Bratunac?

utterances.speaker: SRBISLAV DAVIDOVIC
utterances.text: You're referring to the situation of the 12th in the evening when the buses arrived in Bratunac. There were six buses in total in front of the municipality. I was informed that on a football pitch there were another 20 to 25 buses. I was surprised by that too. Perhaps that's around 9.00 or 10.00 in the evening I met Deronjic. Bratunac is a small town, and the municipal building is in the centre. So the entire area includes 100, 200 metres. And I asked Deronjic, Why are they bringing in so many buses to Bratunac? He literally said, We were being set up by Rajko Dukic. All these buses came from him, from Mile and Kasaba. And he sent them all to Bratunac. Then I told him, Miroslav, try to use your contacts with the government or the president to have the buses taken out of Bratunac, including the people on them. It was around 9.00 or 10.00 in the evening. The next morning, the buses indeed left Bratunac.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: SRBISLAV DAVIDOVIC
utterances.text: Now, I did not ask Miroslav whether he had called anyone to intervene and whether the buses left on those orders or on that intervention, but all I know is that the bus did leave.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Thank you. The remainder of the -- the remaining members of the civilian authorities in Bratunac, did they share your sentiments about the events in Kravica? Was that a shock to them as well, a surprise?

utterances.speaker: SRBISLAV DAVIDOVIC
utterances.text: Well, for everyone there it was a surprise and a shock. At first, people couldn't even believe that something like that could have happened, but it did.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Thank you. Did you hear of people being taken off buses, individual people, or, first of all, do you agree that these civilians left, civilians from Potocari, left towards Kladanj without anyone being taken off the bus?

utterances.speaker: SRBISLAV DAVIDOVIC
utterances.text: Well, at the time, I had not heard about people being taken off buses, not at that time. Perhaps a few months later when people were talking again about and retelling the events there were such instances, but not in Bratunac. On the way to Vlasenica and Kladanj and so on, there were stories that some buses were stopped there and the people were taken off buses, but in Bratunac that did not happen at the time. At least I didn't know of it and I didn't see any such thing.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: If I can intervene. Mr. Davidovic, you referred to Rajko Djukic. Do you remember having said that?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Dukic, D.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: You said, referring to Deronjic, "We were being set up by Rajko Dukic. All these buses came from him, from Milici and Kasaba. And he sent them all to Bratunac." Do you remember having said that?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: And in the Popovic transcript, page 9217, you testified that "Rajko Dukic from Milic is framing -- framing us up." Do you remember having said that also?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I just interpreted verbatim Deronjic's word. He said Rajko Dukic is framing us up with this. He sent his buses from his municipality to Bratunac municipality.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: It's a bit difficult to follow what it meant. Could you tell us who Mr. Dukic was or what he was, and what Deronjic meant by saying so, Rajko Dukic is framing this -- or setting this up. Could you expand a little bit more on that.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Rajko Dukic is from Milici. He was the manager of the bauxite mine, and he was a very influential person both in Milici and in the general area referred to as Birac. I think that in that area he was the most prominent political figure. I believe that he was the man in charge even higher up than Deronjic. Now, whether there were some rivalries between him and Deronjic in the political sense, I don't know, but I don't think that this convoy which he said he had sent towards Bratunac, I don't think it is a reflection of their animosity, the animosity between the two of them. Now, why Deronjic said that this was -- that Rajko Dukic was framing us up, then he would know why he said that. I don't, but I just interpreted his words verbatim. Have I cleared that up a bit?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Yes. I wonder whether you can answer, tell us why or how come Mr. Dukic could send the buses to Bratunac at all.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] My apologies. I can't hear very clearly.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: The witness didn't hear translation.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: My question was how come --

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I cannot hear this. I cannot hear.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Okay. Our usher will assist you.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I can hear you well, but I cannot hear the interpreters, or I can barely hear them.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Mr. Davidovic, do you hear me now well?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I can hear you very well, and I could hear you before as well, but interpreters -- now -- now it's better.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: My question was: How come Mr. Dukic was able to send the buses to Bratunac at all?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Well, I've already said that he was a very prominent person, and he may have a sway over the army as well. That's my assessment.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Thank you. Yes, Mr. Karadzic.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Can I try and clarify this. Is it correct that Muslim soldiers were captured in various woods in Milici, Vlasenica, Cerska, Zvornik, and Kamenica municipalities, and that all those prisoners of war were sent back to Bratunac at the time? So was it in that sense that Deronjic said if they had been captured in Milici, he should have kept them in Milici?

utterances.speaker: SRBISLAV DAVIDOVIC
utterances.text: Well, I believe that the largest number of soldiers were captured in Milici, because the road, or, the route that the Muslims took towards Kladanj and Tuzla went through their municipality.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Thank you. So Deronjic considered that Dukic probably felt that they should not remain in his municipality, although they had been captured there, and that they should be sent and kept in the municipalities where -- and that Deronjic felt that they should be kept where they were captured.

utterances.speaker: SRBISLAV DAVIDOVIC
utterances.text: Well, yes. Why would they be sent to Bratunac?

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Thank you. Well, I don't know if this is clear for the Trial Chamber, but that is how I understood, that they felt -- that he felt they wanted to get rid of these prisoners of war. They didn't want them on the territory of their municipality. Am I correct? Is that more or less the gist of his suspicion that this was a frame-up by Dukic?

utterances.speaker: SRBISLAV DAVIDOVIC
utterances.text: Well, yes. The gist is -- or the point is, you know, I want to just take the burden off my back and put it on someone else's back.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Well, that's a saying, isn't it? That's our saying.

utterances.speaker: SRBISLAV DAVIDOVIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Very well. Thank you. Now, you then heard that some of those prisoners were held at the school building and that after the evacuation it turned out that there were people killed and that bodies were found in almost all of these classrooms, and that, too, was a shock?

utterances.speaker: SRBISLAV DAVIDOVIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: And do you remember that the civilian protection and the utilities, the public utilities company that also deal with funerals, that they then buried these men?

utterances.speaker: SRBISLAV DAVIDOVIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: When did you learn, aside from the media and various rumours that were going around, when did you learn that there were some killings on route to Batkovici?

utterances.speaker: SRBISLAV DAVIDOVIC
utterances.text: Well, some 10 days or so later, 10 to 15 days later.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Do you believe those rumours?

utterances.speaker: SRBISLAV DAVIDOVIC
utterances.text: Unfortunately, yes, because I heard this from competent, to put it this way, people that that was done.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Thank you. Now, can you confirm for the Trial Chamber that Batkovic as a co-operative and a prison for prisoners of war was near Bijeljina and that in order to get to -- if you wanted to get from Bratunac to Batkovic you would have to get through Konjevic Polje, Zvornik, and so on?

utterances.speaker: SRBISLAV DAVIDOVIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Thank you. Now, when the buses set out towards Zvornik, towards Batkovici, did you and other people around you believe that they would end up in Batkovic?

utterances.speaker: SRBISLAV DAVIDOVIC
utterances.text: Well, I didn't really investigate that, but I was told by this police officer that they were going for Batkovic, but whether that actually happened or not, I don't know.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Thank you. Now, I'd like to ask you this: Did you ever hear from any Serb, any official or any outsider, did you ever see or sense or learn that they wanted to eradicate Muslims, to kick them out of there, or to do anything to them that they wouldn't want to be done unto them?

utterances.speaker: SRBISLAV DAVIDOVIC
utterances.text: Never. At the meeting on the 12th, I learnt that it would be carried out properly as agreed at the meeting, and I was even regaled by what the commander of the Dutch Battalion said, who said that he had received an order from his command or his government to take part in the organisation of this transport of Muslims towards Kladanj, and the meeting was already wrapping up, we were all standing, and at that point even Mladic said, Well, I'll provide the buses, you take care of the fuel. So it ended up on a more positive note, if I can put it that way, and I was convince that that's how it would be carried out, but of course the story's different now.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Thank you. Now, do you agree that the entire Serb population, including the authorities, as well as the parties, Serb parties, differed significantly in their position vis-a-vis various Muslims? In other words, is it correct that Serbs did not have a problem with Muslims per se, but that they also had close ties with Zulfikarpasic and other Muslims?

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: The interpreter did if the hear the other names.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Just as you had good relations with Muslims in the town itself, whereas the extremist were in the surrounding villages?

utterances.speaker: SRBISLAV DAVIDOVIC
utterances.text: Well, I'm sure Muhamed Filipovic and Adil Zulfikarpasic were -- or, had followed the softer line than the SDA, and according to us, our sense was that it would be easier to reach a compromise with them than with the SDA.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Thank you. Well, I just wanted to show here, were Serbs against Muslims or against fundamentalism?

utterances.speaker: SRBISLAV DAVIDOVIC
utterances.text: Well, absolutely. Not at one point -- I never thought that they were against Muslims as an ethnicity, but they were against fundamentalism.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. Davidovic, and my apologies if I was not precise enough, but thank you for your efficient answers to my cross-examination.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I have no further questions, Your Excellency, and I've completed my examination three minutes before time. So I would really appreciate being applauded here, because usually I go too far and I step over my time limit.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Thank you. Ms. West, do you have re-examination?

utterances.speaker: MS. WEST
utterances.text: I do, Mr. President, and I wonder if the Court would agree to take the break now and indulge me with this time.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: How long?

utterances.speaker: MS. WEST
utterances.text: I suspect it will be at least 20 minutes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: We'll have the break.

utterances.speaker: MS. WEST
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Then we'll have a break for an hour and resume at 1.20. --- Luncheon recess taken at 12.20 p.m.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Yes, Ms. West.

utterances.speaker: MS. WEST
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. President.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Just a second.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BAIRD
utterances.text: Ms. West, just one question, please bear with me.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BAIRD
utterances.text: Mr. Davidovic, I would like to take you back to the evidence you gave just before the break. Dr. Karadzic asked you: "You heard that some of these prisoners were held at the school building and that after the evacuation it turn out that people were killed and there were bodies in almost all of these classrooms, and that, too, was a shock." And your answer was: "Yes." Do you recollect this?

utterances.speaker: SRBISLAV DAVIDOVIC
utterances.text: Yes, I do.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BAIRD
utterances.text: Now, can you tell us who were those people who were killed and their bodies were in the classroom?

utterances.speaker: SRBISLAV DAVIDOVIC
utterances.text: The people who were killed were Muslims, and their bodies were in classrooms.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BAIRD
utterances.text: Were they -- were they prisoners of war?

utterances.speaker: SRBISLAV DAVIDOVIC
utterances.text: I don't know their origins. I don't know how to classify them, but for the most part these were people who had lived in Srebrenica, in that area. Now, as to who brought them there and how they happened to be there, I don't know about that.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BAIRD
utterances.text: Thank you. Yes, Ms. West.

utterances.speaker: MS. WEST
utterances.text: Thank you, Your Honour. May I have 65 ter 16205, please.

utterances.speaker: MS. WEST
utterances.text: Mr. Davidovic, on page 54 today you mentioned a gentleman who's name was Omo Jahic as the man who was on the bus. Do you remember that?

utterances.speaker: SRBISLAV DAVIDOVIC
utterances.text: Yes, I do. His name was not Omer but Omo, O-m-o, just three letters.

utterances.speaker: MS. WEST
utterances.text: Thank you. And could you spell his last name, please?

utterances.speaker: SRBISLAV DAVIDOVIC
utterances.text: Do you want me to spell it? J-a-h-i-c. J-a-h-i-c, five letters.

utterances.speaker: MS. WEST
utterances.text: And do you know his father's name?

utterances.speaker: SRBISLAV DAVIDOVIC
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: MS. WEST
utterances.text: And today --

utterances.speaker: SRBISLAV DAVIDOVIC
utterances.text: He was about 50 to 55 years old, that man.

utterances.speaker: MS. WEST
utterances.text: Okay. Thank you very much. And today at page 63, you were talking about killings on the route to Batkovici, and the question was: "Do you believe those rumours?" And your answer was: "Unfortunately, yes, because I heard this from competent, to put it this way, people that that was done." Can you please tell us from whom you heard this.

utterances.speaker: SRBISLAV DAVIDOVIC
utterances.text: Well, I don't know if I said that this was on the way to Fakovici, because Fakovici are in the opposite direction. They are not downstream but upstream, up the Drina River, but maybe that's not even important. I heard that -- no, I'm not really clear on what you mean by Fakovici. I believe I did not mention Fakovici in this context.

utterances.speaker: MS. WEST
utterances.text: You're right, you didn't. You said -- my fault. You said Batkovici.

utterances.speaker: SRBISLAV DAVIDOVIC
utterances.text: Oh, sorry, so that's Batkovici. Batkovici is a town you get to via Konjevic Polje, Zvornik, and it is in the Bijeljina municipality. I didn't hear that they were killed in Batkovici but, rather, en route from Zvornik to Batkovici. I heard that. I mean, there were rumours in town. I heard from people who were members of the army that these things had happened, but I couldn't really say that I heard this from people who would spread rumours. Rather, this is something that actually did happen. There was mention of Kozluk, Celopek, Pilica.

utterances.speaker: MS. WEST
utterances.text: Okay. So if I should understand correctly, you don't remember the actual names of the people who told you this, but you remember those people were trustworthy.

utterances.speaker: SRBISLAV DAVIDOVIC
utterances.text: Exactly.

utterances.speaker: MS. WEST
utterances.text: So now we have 65 ter 16205 in front of us, and I want to talk to you about this in regard to your testimony on page 48 today. On page 48, you indicated that the bus had not been mobilised by the 10.00 meeting, and that would be the 10.00 meeting at the Hotel Fontana on the 12th. So I'd like to go through this together. This is a document from the 12th of July, Zvornik public security centre. And number 1 says: Acting in accordance with your dispatch, I contacted the civilian commissioner in Bratunac, Miroslav Deronjic. Number 2: A meeting with Mladic and Krstic was held at the Bratunac Brigade headquarters at 8.00 at which tasks were assigned to all those involved. Now, you were at a meeting with Mladic at 8.00 at the Bratunac Brigade headquarters; right?

utterances.speaker: SRBISLAV DAVIDOVIC
utterances.text: I think this is not a reference to that meeting, because there were no tasks assigned, and General Krstic was not present, and he is mentioned here.

utterances.speaker: MS. WEST
utterances.text: Okay.

utterances.speaker: SRBISLAV DAVIDOVIC
utterances.text: I believe this is not about that meeting, not at the meeting with Mladic at 8.00.

utterances.speaker: MS. WEST
utterances.text: Okay. Well, notwithstanding those two facts, you indeed did meet with Mladic at 8.00 that morning at the Bratunac Brigade headquarters; correct?

utterances.speaker: SRBISLAV DAVIDOVIC
utterances.text: Yes, correct.

utterances.speaker: MS. WEST
utterances.text: And number 3: The military operation is continuing according to plan. The Turks are fleeing ... while the civilians have gathered in Potocari, about 15.000. 4: Consultations are underway to appoint the chief of the public security situation in Srebrenica and the commander of the police station in Srebrenica and select 15 policemen from the ranks who along with the newly elected president of Srebrenica, the chairman of the Srebrenica Executive Board and priests will immediately take over all important facilities in the town. Sir, my question for you is whether at this -- looking at number 4, does this sound to you that planning and decisions were already well underway by that point, by the time this document was written?

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Could we please be shown a better copy, because I'm not sure the translation is correct. I don't think that what we see in English here is actually consistent with what it says in Serbian, because it's out of the question that a priest would take over the Executive Board. There must be something -- some mistake there.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Ms. West.

utterances.speaker: MS. WEST
utterances.text: Your Honour, I don't have a better version, but if -- if the concern is the issue with the priests, I can take that part out of my question.

utterances.speaker: MS. WEST
utterances.text: So, Mr. Davidovic, assuming take the priest part out, does that sound to you, the things that I read off, that the planning and decisions were already well underway by the writing of this document?

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Well, my apologies, but I would also like to know what other mistakes there may be in translation other than the priest issue, because the -- the text in Serbian is not quite legible.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: While we can following the English on our personal computer, why don't we zoom in in the Serbian, B/C/S version. A bit farther.

utterances.speaker: MS. WEST
utterances.text: Does that help you, Mr. Davidovic?

utterances.speaker: SRBISLAV DAVIDOVIC
utterances.text: Well, yes. This is a bit better, but I have never seen this letter before. As far as I could see from the heading, this was sent from the police station in Bijeljina to the Ministry of the Interior at Pale. And they're reporting on some of their activities, or some activities that I knew nothing about, nor was I ever informed of anything of that sort.

utterances.speaker: MS. WEST
utterances.text: Well, at that time, at 8.00 in the morning on the 12th, you were aware that there were events going on in Potocari and Srebrenica; correct?

utterances.speaker: MR. ROBINSON
utterances.text: Objection, leading.

utterances.speaker: MS. WEST
utterances.text: I can rephrase.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. WEST
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MS. WEST
utterances.text: On the morning of the 12th, what was your understanding as to what was going on with the refugees from Srebrenica in Potocari?

utterances.speaker: SRBISLAV DAVIDOVIC
utterances.text: At the time, I didn't even know that there were refugees in Potocari at 8.00 in the morning. I only learned of that at the meeting at the Fontana Hotel at 10.00, I learned the fact that there were refugees in Potocari.

utterances.speaker: MS. WEST
utterances.text: All right. And we move to number 5 which talks about that meeting you attended: A meeting will begin at 10.00 that morning with representatives of the UNPROFOR and the International Red Cross and the Muslim representative of Srebrenica at which an agreement will be reached on the evacuation of the civilian population from Potocari to Kladanj. So let's stop there. Indeed, you went to a 10.00 meeting; right?

utterances.speaker: SRBISLAV DAVIDOVIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. WEST
utterances.text: And would you agree with me that as regards this document, it appears that it had to have been written before that 10.00 meeting?

utterances.speaker: SRBISLAV DAVIDOVIC
utterances.text: Well, I couldn't really comment on that. I really don't know anything about that. This is the first time that I see this, and I see that it's the police station in Bijeljina and the ministry. I don't really know.

utterances.speaker: MS. WEST
utterances.text: Mr. President, we do have a better version of this document. I think if you unlock or --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Shall we put it on the [overlapping speakers]

utterances.speaker: MS. WEST
utterances.text: We can upload it. One moment, please.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Could I ask Ms. West to ask the witness how far Bijeljina is from Bratunac. Perhaps we should establish that as well.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: We can know that from any map. Yes. I think this is better. Yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. WEST
utterances.text: Thank you very much. Thank you, Mr. Reid.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Why don't we ask the witness to read the para -- para 5, in particular those in parentheses, because English translation says it was illegible.

utterances.speaker: MS. WEST
utterances.text: Sir, if you can go ahead and read both 4 and 5, please.

utterances.speaker: SRBISLAV DAVIDOVIC
utterances.text: The fourth paragraph: "An agreement is underway on appointing the chief of the public security station in Srebrenica and the commander of the police station Srebrenica, as well as a selection of 15 police officers from the VRS who would, together with the newly appointed president of the Srebrenica municipality and the president of the Executive Committee of Srebrenica as well as priests, immediately take control of all significant buildings in the city." Paragraph 5: "At 10.00, a meeting with representatives of the UNPROFOR, International Red Cross, and Muslim representatives from Srebrenica has begun, and an agreement on the evacuation of all civilian populations from Potocari to Kladanj has been reached." And then in parentheses: "(So that they would have more problems there.)" This is not logical. What it says in parentheses is that so that they should have more problems there or more difficulties there.

utterances.speaker: MS. WEST
utterances.text: Okay.

utterances.speaker: SRBISLAV DAVIDOVIC
utterances.text: "One hundred trailer trucks for transport have already been assigned."

utterances.speaker: MS. WEST
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. Davidovic. So we'll go to --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: So the translation is not the meeting will begin at 10.00. The meeting has begun. Did you notice the difference in interpretation.

utterances.speaker: MS. WEST
utterances.text: If we can have him read it again. I didn't see that there.

utterances.speaker: MS. WEST
utterances.text: Sir, can you read the beginning of paragraph 5 again?

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: Interpreter's note: In Serbian, it is -- it could be interpreted in either way. Either will begin or has begun.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] "At 10.00 a meeting has begun or will begin with representatives of the UNPROFOR and International Red Cross. At 10.00, a meeting is beginning."

utterances.speaker: MS. WEST
utterances.text: Okay. Fair enough. But that -- that paragraph goes on, "At 10.00 the meeting is beginning," and it goes on, it says, regarding the agreement of the evacuation of all civilian population from Potocari. Sir, when we talked to you about the meeting at 8.00 -- or when you spoke about the meeting at 8.00 and then the 10.00 meeting that you went to, you indicated to the Court that the evacuation of the Muslims from Potocari had not yet been decided, that in fact they had been given -- they would be given a choice. So how do you rectify this paragraph with your own testimony?

utterances.speaker: SRBISLAV DAVIDOVIC
utterances.text: I've said that at the meeting at 10.00, I realised that there was an earlier meeting where only the president was present. That Mancic, Nesib, and no agreement had been reached at that meeting. So at this new meeting, the third meeting at 10.00, a delegation of Muslims arrived. There was larger number of people together with Nesib Mancic. There was also Ibro Nuhanovic and --

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: The interpreter did not hear the third name.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] And they came with a proposal that they had decided on in Srebrenica. So at this second meeting, in my view, Nesib could not could not say either way we are leaving or we are staying. I believe he had to go for consultations to Srebrenica, and then he returned later on to this meeting, the three of them, and they told them -- they told us what they had decided.

utterances.speaker: MS. WEST
utterances.text: But in regard to that meeting at page 48 you also said that the buses had not been mobilised by the 10.00 a.m. meeting, and then page 53, you said, when the meeting concluded at 11.30 that's when transport was sought and the buses arrived. But let's go back to this document. You just read that a hundred trailer trucks have been provided for transport. Mr. Davidovic, would you agree with this document, or I will ask for your comment as to the inconsistency with your testimony. Do you agree that the buses and transport had already been prepared?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Let me -- let me clarify this. Is it your position that this document was written before the meeting?

utterances.speaker: MS. WEST
utterances.text: My position is that it was written before or just as the meeting was happening, the 10.00 meeting.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Immediately after the meeting.

utterances.speaker: MS. WEST
utterances.text: Mr. Davidovic's testimony --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Could you -- could you repeat what you said? It was before or just as the meeting was happening?

utterances.speaker: MS. WEST
utterances.text: If -- if -- the question is when this document was created.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: So it will depend upon the interpretation of the -- of para 5.

utterances.speaker: MS. WEST
utterances.text: Right, which is the --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: And according to what Mr. Davidovic read, it was translated as the agreement has been reached. Line 21, page 72. So before going further, I want that part to be clarified first.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Well, if I may. Here there is just a projection of what kind of agreement will be reached, because it says here at 10.00 a meeting begins with the UNPROFOR members and members of the International Committee of the Red Cross as well as Muslim representatives from Srebrenica where an agreement on evacuation is to be or will be reached. So that would imply that that was about to happen that --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Hmm. Very well.

utterances.speaker: MS. WEST
utterances.text: Thank you very much, Mr. Davidovic. Let's go back to the trucks, the hundred trailer trucks that have been provided for transport. Would you agree that at the writing of this document the mobilisation of trucks had already begun?

utterances.speaker: SRBISLAV DAVIDOVIC
utterances.text: I've already said that this meeting ended at around 11.00 or a bit after 11.00. It ended hastily in a way, and this is why: Somebody came into the room where the meeting was being held and said that the population in Potocari was getting restless and that there was a threat that -- there was a fear that the people, the civilian population, the people will set out from Potocari towards Bratunac on foot, which would be a disaster, because if 10.000 people were to move, you can imagine. So in a way the meeting was hastily wrapped up to prevent this from happening, and they wanted the delegation to get back to Potocari and tell them that there would be transportation provided. As for these 100 trailer trucks, I don't know that there were as many. No one talked about it at the meeting, nor do I know who it was who provided all these vehicles. Probably the military. We had no influence on that, nor did anyone ask us to do anything in that respect. We were just asked to be humane, but nobody asked us for any vehicles or fuel or anything like that.

utterances.speaker: MS. WEST
utterances.text: Mr. Davidovic, at line [sic] 76 and 7, you said that the people -- there was a concern that the people would set out from Potocari towards Bratunac on foot and so then it appears that the meeting ended hastily. I'm not familiar with that. Have you testified to that before, in your memory?

utterances.speaker: SRBISLAV DAVIDOVIC
utterances.text: Yes, I have.

utterances.speaker: MS. WEST
utterances.text: Okay.

utterances.speaker: MS. WEST
utterances.text: Your Honour, I'd like to tender this document.

utterances.speaker: MR. ROBINSON
utterances.text: Objection, Mr. President.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Yes, Mr. Robinson.

utterances.speaker: MR. ROBINSON
utterances.text: The witness hasn't confirmed anything about the document.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Ms. West.

utterances.speaker: MS. WEST
utterances.text: The witness indeed confirmed that he was at an 8.00 meeting with General Mladic at the Bratunac Brigade headquarters. That is the second paragraph. He indicates that he didn't see Krstic and no tasks were assigned. I think it's very possible that tasks were assigned afterwards, but this document deals with the very same subject matter that that witness testified to at his own meeting. I think the witness has documents authenticated, but I think the witness is certainly making it reliable and certainly relevant.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] May I add something?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Yes, Mr. --

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honour, may I add something?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Yes, Mr. Davidovic.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] At the meeting at 8.00, those who were there, Simatovic, Aco Tesic, and I, we were there for about 20 minutes, then we left. So around 20 minutes. We left the command when we were told to attend a meeting at 10.00, Simic and I. Maybe the meeting was resumed following our departure, but we were no longer there. Perhaps at 8.30 Krstic indeed arrived and they continued with the meeting, but we were no longer there.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Mr. Davidovic also testified about attending 10.00 meeting in that regard. This document may help us -- contextualise that part of his evidence. In that regard, we will admit this.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: As Exhibit P4373.

utterances.speaker: MS. WEST
utterances.text: May I have 65 ter 30940A. Sorry.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: I'm sorry. We will admit only the first page. Only that document. It consists of four or five documents. Yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. WEST
utterances.text: Mr. Davidovic, before we leave this issue about buses as regards your testimony that they had not been mobilised by the time of the Hotel Fontana meeting, I'd like to show you this: This is an intercept from 12 July at 7.35 in the morning, and it's --

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [No interpretation].

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: I'm sorry, Mr. Karadzic?

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Objection. Please, language is of utmost importance here. If something is stated as being provided, it doesn't mean it was commandeered or mobilised. "Provided" means that there was information where vehicles were, but they were not mobilised. Perhaps you can ask the witness to distinguish between the two words.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Thank you. Ms. West would be happy to reformulate the question.

utterances.speaker: MS. WEST
utterances.text: Thank you, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Sorry. It also affects the previous document, which says "provided." In other words, they had information where to find those assets rather than them being mobilised already.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: That's sufficient. Yes, Ms. West.

utterances.speaker: MS. WEST
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. President.

utterances.speaker: MS. WEST
utterances.text: This regards today's testimony when you spoke about buses, and this is an intercept July 12th. It's between Krstic who at that time was still the Chief of Staff, and Krsmanovic who was head of transportation. And we'll just read this. It's quite short: "Krstic: Hello, is that Krsmanovic? "X: Yes, go ahead. "K: Listen write this down. "X: Yes. "K: Now, Pale, Visegrad, Rogatica, Sokolac, Han Pijesak, Vlasenica, Milici, Bratunac, Zvornik. Now, this from all these places, 50 buses in total are to be at the stadium in Bratunac by 1700 hours. "X: At 1700 hours at the Bratunac stadium. "K: Make very sure this is done. Is that clear? "X: Understood. "K: Go ahead." Mr. Davidovic, my question for you regards the night of the 12th. You testified today that there were several buses in the town of Bratunac. You, yourself, saw at least 6 and then you had information that there were 20 to 25 at the stadium. Can you tell the Trial Chamber, if you know, how early did all those buses arrive in Bratunac?

utterances.speaker: SRBISLAV DAVIDOVIC
utterances.text: I think this intercept does not discuss the buses I mentioned.

utterances.speaker: MS. WEST
utterances.text: And why -- go ahead.

utterances.speaker: SRBISLAV DAVIDOVIC
utterances.text: The buses I discussed arrived in front of the municipal building between 8.00 and 8.30 p.m.

utterances.speaker: MS. WEST
utterances.text: And prior to that period of time, during the day did you see any other buses in Bratunac?

utterances.speaker: SRBISLAV DAVIDOVIC
utterances.text: I did not.

utterances.speaker: MS. WEST
utterances.text: And for some of that day you were in Potocari; correct?

utterances.speaker: SRBISLAV DAVIDOVIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. WEST
utterances.text: Go ahead.

utterances.speaker: SRBISLAV DAVIDOVIC
utterances.text: I was in Potocari perhaps between 2.00 and 4.00 p.m.

utterances.speaker: MS. WEST
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MS. WEST
utterances.text: Mr. President, in regard to the issue of the term "mobilised," I used the term because I was reciting the witness's testimony today, and he said: "If I say that up until then it was uncertain"--

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Page?

utterances.speaker: MS. WEST
utterances.text: Forty-eight. Excuse me, excuse me. The question is this: "Am I right if I say that up until then it was uncertain whether they would leave and until then buses had not been mobilised, and no one realised that they would leave for sure?" And the answer was: "I did not know that that would happen." But, Your Honour --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Did you say page 48?

utterances.speaker: MS. WEST
utterances.text: Page 48 of today's transcript, lines 14 through 17.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Seven to -- I'm sorry, I couldn't find it. Let us proceed.

utterances.speaker: MS. WEST
utterances.text: Okay. And may this document be marked for identification.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: I'm not sure whether witness has given any foundation about this document. At the moment, could you tender it at a later stage?

utterances.speaker: MS. WEST
utterances.text: Yes, Mr. President.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. WEST
utterances.text: Mr. Davidovic, I'm going to draw your attention to other testimony today. At page 15, you were talking about the date of April 17th, 1992, and you were talking about paramilitaries who appeared at that time for the first time in Bratunac, and you said once they arrived, the harassment and mistreatment of the Muslims began. Do you remember that testimony?

utterances.speaker: SRBISLAV DAVIDOVIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. WEST
utterances.text: And is it your position that the -- the harassment of Muslims during that period of time were to be blamed on the paramilitary groups who came to Bratunac?

utterances.speaker: SRBISLAV DAVIDOVIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. WEST
utterances.text: And is it your testimony that the Bratunac leadership was not co-operating or co-ordinating with these paramilitary groups or were not involved with the paramilitaries' presence in Bratunac?

utterances.speaker: SRBISLAV DAVIDOVIC
utterances.text: As far as I know, they were not.

utterances.speaker: MS. WEST
utterances.text: Okay.

utterances.speaker: MS. WEST
utterances.text: 65 ter, please, number 23611. If we can go to page 5, please. It begins with "Factual Basis."

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Objection.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: On what basis, Mr. Karadzic?

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] On the basis that this material, 92 quater, was not admitted in my case and is part of the plea agreement in question. I don't think it should be relied on in this case.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: What's the problem with putting a passage in the document to the witness?

utterances.speaker: MR. ROBINSON
utterances.text: Well, Mr. President, this is actually attempting to use the statements of this witness, and you've already found that it is unfair for those statements to be used at this trial. So I don't see why it would be legitimate to put a statement which has been excluded to the witness.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: She's not tendering this document as evidence.

utterances.speaker: MR. ROBINSON
utterances.text: Well, that's true, but by -- she's using the statement essentially to impeach this statement. So she's making derivative use of the statement. I also think, Mr. President, while we're on this subject that before she proceeds any further, she should have to state her -- put her case to the witness, because she's now cross-examining him, and she should be required to put her case first and then not use any document which has previously been excluded. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Would you like to respond, Ms. West?

utterances.speaker: MS. WEST
utterances.text: Your Honour, I'm not cross-examining this witness. I specifically am avoiding using those types of questions. I'm trying to elicit information about the subject matters this witness brought up on cross-examination to elicit more information, which is exactly what I plan to do with the statement. The witness can agree with these facts or not agree with these facts, and he can also provide us more information. I've not moved to admit this statement.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Are you not going to contradict what the witness early on?

utterances.speaker: MS. WEST
utterances.text: I mean, I asked the witness whether the information in this statement is consistent with his own memory and some of it will be, I suspect, based on what he has said and ask him to explain in those situations where it's not. I'm not sure what this witness will say about that, but I think it will be helpful to the Trial Chamber.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Very well.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: There are some unclear parts, but the Chamber sees your line of question is -- is to contradict what witness said, so -- but in any event, the Chamber will allow you to continue and that -- even if the document is -- was not admitted or is not going to be admitted, I don't see any problem in asking a question as to whether witness agrees with a certain part of the document. Please carry on.

utterances.speaker: MR. ROBINSON
utterances.text: Excuse me, Mr. President. If the witness agrees with a certain part of the document, then isn't the Prosecutor getting in through the back door what you --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: No, you can ask -- cross-examine the witness based upon the witness's evidence. We do not -- going to admit this document.

utterances.speaker: MR. ROBINSON
utterances.text: No, it doesn't matter whether you admit it or not. If someone affirms the content of the document, it wouldn't make any difference whether you've admitted the document or not. The substance will have been admitted. I was wondering maybe if we could have this conversation outside the presence of this witness, because I would think if we think it through as to what the possibilities are, it might be better if the witness isn't hearing that, but if you think about what -- I would like to know, for example, which paragraphs she wants to put to this witness and if he confirms it. That's one thing. If he -- if it contradicts then it may be another matter, but I don't think we should discuss that in front of the witness.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Has the -- I will refrain. Just a second.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: My apologies, Mr. Davidovic. If you could excuse yourself for a moment. The Chamber will discuss some procedural issues.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: How shall we start? First of all, Ms. West, why did you need Deronjic's plea agreement or factual basis to put a certain question to the witness?

utterances.speaker: MS. WEST
utterances.text: The -- the witness himself brought up a -- a number of items that are in this plea agreement -- excuse me, the factual basis for the plea agreement. It is a very good chronology of what was going on in Bratunac at the time. It is a good basis by which to see -- to explore with this witness what are the actual facts. It is just another document. And I would suggest to the Court that it really -- it would be as if I were taking the statement of another witness and showing it to this witness --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Why could she not ask him independently of any other documents?

utterances.speaker: MS. WEST
utterances.text: Your Honour, I think I could do that as well, but I think this Court has specifically allowed under its May 19th, 2010, decision that parties may confront a witness in court with the witness statement or transcript of prior testimony of another witness from another case. I would submit that this factual basis is no more than another statement of a witness.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: So you are confront -- you would like to confront your witness?

utterances.speaker: MS. WEST
utterances.text: I'm not sure that I would use the word confront because I'm not sure what this witness will say. I want to ask him about some of the facts in here to see if he can provide us any more information. This all came up during the cross-examination of this witness. This did not come up as part of the direct, and this is directly in response to that.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: What part of the document are you going to put to the witness? What topics are there?

utterances.speaker: MS. WEST
utterances.text: The topics that I expect to talk about are specifically the paramilitaries that he spoke about in --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Para numbers?

utterances.speaker: MS. WEST
utterances.text: Yes. In particular, paragraph 14.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Okay. Shall we move to ...

utterances.speaker: MS. WEST
utterances.text: That's -- yes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Fourteen, yes, and --

utterances.speaker: MS. WEST
utterances.text: Fourteen, 15, and 16, and they all concern the subject matter.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Yes. Paramilitaries. And then?

utterances.speaker: MS. WEST
utterances.text: And then --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Is that it?

utterances.speaker: MS. WEST
utterances.text: I'm sorry. No. There's 27, 28, 29. This all regards the killing of Goran Zekic who the witness indicated was killed right before the attack on Glogova. And that's all.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Twenty-seven to --

utterances.speaker: MS. WEST
utterances.text: Twenty-nine.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Twenty-nine. Killing of Goran Zekic.

utterances.speaker: MS. WEST
utterances.text: And Glogova.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Yes, Mr. Robinson.

utterances.speaker: MR. ROBINSON
utterances.text: Yes, Mr. President. I think one -- one way to resolve this is looking at the substance. Paragraphs 14 through 16 don't seem to make the point that she was asking the witness to contradict, that the paramilitaries were working without the -- or against the wishes of the city, the municipal leaders. That was her question essentially, or that's his testimony that she's trying to contradict. Those paragraphs don't, to me, seem to directly go to that issue. Similarly, paragraph 27 to 29, particularly paragraph 29, talks about an attack against Glogova which is outside of the scope of the examination. And I don't believe would be permitted in any event. And I don't see anything in paragraphs 27 or 28 that's in any way inconsistent with the witness's testimony or that she couldn't ask him without reference to this document. But, essentially, if you look at paragraph 13 of the document, this is the tenor in which this witness was giving information during his plea agreement which he was attempting to negotiate for a good disposition of his case. I don't think that having -- this is different than putting a witness statement to a witness. This is material which has already been ruled will not be admissible because it would be unfair. So to put it -- for the very negligible benefit that the Prosecution might get of showing this document to the witness and asking questions based on this document given the subject matters that she's identified, the prejudice to Dr. Karadzic even from discussing this document outweighs any benefit. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Even if she were to now allow put questions about paragraph 13. Yes, Ms. West, would you like to reply if any?

utterances.speaker: MS. WEST
utterances.text: Just briefly, Your Honour. But in regard to 14, 15, and 16, the witness had indicated that -- on page 23 today that no one had advocated the expelling of Muslims, and I want to know a little bit more about that. And then very specifically the witness spoke about this 17 April rally or meeting - I'm not sure what it was called - of volunteers who entered in Bratunac. That is also mentioned here and I want to see what he has to say about that. I don't think this goes beyond any -- any normal procedure by which we should be allowed to develop subject matters that came up during cross-examination. I just happen to be using this piece of paper to do it. If this were the statement of another witness or document I suspect I would be allowed to do that.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: And about Glogova?

utterances.speaker: MS. WEST
utterances.text: Sorry, yes. The witness indicated that Glogova was in retaliation for the killing of Goran Zekic, and that's 27 -- well, that's talked about in 27, 28, and 29, and I wanted to know whether he had any more information about that. He was -- he was brief about it but he spoke about Glogova.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BAIRD
utterances.text: Ms. West, the fact that the material was already ruled inadmissible would have no bearing at all on the situation?

utterances.speaker: MS. WEST
utterances.text: I don't believe it would, Your Honour, because there are times where we can show witnesses documents that are not the witness's, that have nothing to do with the witness, and if it's relevant and if he point something out on a document that helps him explain something to the Trial Chamber, we would be allowed to do this. I agree this has not been admitted by this Court, but it is perfectly relevant to what he brought up on cross-examination and, again, I'm not asking for its admission. I'm asking it to be used as an aid to elicit more testimony on these subject matters.

utterances.speaker: MR. ROBINSON
utterances.text: But, Mr. President, think about if you had excluded an involuntary confession of a suspect. Ms. West could make the same argument: While would not being admitted into evidence, I just want to see what the witness says about it. That wouldn't hold. This is a situation where you have information which you ruled is not fair to be presented to the trier of fact, or to be introduced at the trial. And she's really just using this as a vehicle for introducing something that you've already ruled should be excluded. She can put her questions about this topic without reference to this document. The fact that she's chosen to do it with this document is simply because she wants to get information that otherwise would not be able to be used.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Unless it's necessary, yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: Well, I don't know how necessary it is. I just -- I do need to point out that Mr. Robinson is conflating two issues and one is the inadmissibility under Rule 95 which is -- which is a completely different matter and entails different considerations to the Court in terms of the use of the document, and the other is whether or not a document is going to be admitted pursuant to Rule 92 which are quite different consideration, so that's, I think, I -- it's important to point that out and I'm sorry to take the Court's time any further with that.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MORRISON
utterances.text: None of this would have arisen had Dr. Karadzic not chosen to raise the issues in cross-examination, and a lawyer would realise the consequences of that.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MORRISON
utterances.text: Yes. By a majority decision, not including the President, Judge Kwon, we take the view that the material can be utilised to formulate a question but without the use of the document per se. Now, Ms. West, do you need time to formulate your questions without direct reference to the document?

utterances.speaker: MS. WEST
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MORRISON
utterances.text: Okay.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Thank you. Let us bring in the witness.

utterances.speaker: MS. WEST
utterances.text: Mr. President, may I proceed?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Yes, please.

utterances.speaker: MS. WEST
utterances.text: Mr. Davidovic, I want to ask you some questions about the paramilitaries that you spoke about earlier who were in the area of Bratunac in 1992. Do you know from where they came?

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: Kindly slow down for the sake of the interpreters, please. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] From Serbia.

utterances.speaker: MS. WEST
utterances.text: And do you know what their purpose was for coming?

utterances.speaker: SRBISLAV DAVIDOVIC
utterances.text: I don't. They do.

utterances.speaker: MS. WEST
utterances.text: And about how long were they there?

utterances.speaker: SRBISLAV DAVIDOVIC
utterances.text: Until they were killed. None of them left alive. They were there at least a month.

utterances.speaker: MS. WEST
utterances.text: And before they arrived, before that month as compared to after that month, had a number of Muslim people left the area?

utterances.speaker: SRBISLAV DAVIDOVIC
utterances.text: Yes, they did.

utterances.speaker: MS. WEST
utterances.text: Now, you also spoke about April 17th. I think you said you were in town and at the Hotel Fontana, and you saw a number of these volunteers. You indicated that you saw Deronjic there as well. Do you remember that?

utterances.speaker: SRBISLAV DAVIDOVIC
utterances.text: I do. In front of the shopping centre at the entrance. Deronjic was there with a lot of other people, mostly Muslims. The volunteers were on the Hotel Fontana terrace in a line of about 30 to 40 metres.

utterances.speaker: MS. WEST
utterances.text: And you spoke about an interaction between Deronjic and I thought what I understood was a Muslim person. Did you see Deronjic speak to any of these paramilitaries at all? Excuse me, strike that. I think I misspoke. You spoke about Deronjic speaking to a person who lived in the town. My question is: Did you see Deronjic speak to any of the paramilitaries?

utterances.speaker: SRBISLAV DAVIDOVIC
utterances.text: I did not.

utterances.speaker: MS. WEST
utterances.text: And do you -- do you -- how long were you in that area?

utterances.speaker: SRBISLAV DAVIDOVIC
utterances.text: You mean when I saw -- 10 to 15 minutes.

utterances.speaker: MS. WEST
utterances.text: Okay. And after 10 to 15 minutes then did you leave?

utterances.speaker: SRBISLAV DAVIDOVIC
utterances.text: I went away, probably home.

utterances.speaker: MS. WEST
utterances.text: Now, you also on cross-examination spoke about a number of incidents where the -- these volunteers were -- were harassing Muslims. You also mentioned Serbs. Do you know of any specific incidences of intimidation or killing of the Bosnian Muslims by these volunteers?

utterances.speaker: SRBISLAV DAVIDOVIC
utterances.text: There were such instances, yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. WEST
utterances.text: And as a result of that, did a number of Bosnian Muslims flee from the municipality of Bratunac?

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Please, I have an intervention for the transcript. The interpretation was that there was a lot of that, whereas the witness said "there was that." [In English] It would be more properly could be translated: There were those kind of things happening.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Very well. Mr. Davidovic, could you repeat your answer to the question whether you knew of any specific incidences of intimidation or killing of the Bosnian Muslims by these volunteers.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] It started -- they began coming to people's homes, bringing them to the school, mistreating them, robbing them.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Very well. I will ask the CLSS to -- to hear again what witness said in line 8 of page 91. Having said that, let's continue.

utterances.speaker: MS. WEST
utterances.text: And so my question is: As a result of that, did a number of Bosnian Muslims flee from the municipality of Bratunac?

utterances.speaker: SRBISLAV DAVIDOVIC
utterances.text: Definitely.

utterances.speaker: MS. WEST
utterances.text: Now, you also spoke about the killing of Goran Zekic, which happened in May, May 8th of 1992, and you spoke about -- that he was --

utterances.speaker: SRBISLAV DAVIDOVIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. WEST
utterances.text: That he was a well respected man. He was beloved by the community.

utterances.speaker: SRBISLAV DAVIDOVIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. WEST
