utterances.text: Now, do you know whether later that same day there was any meeting of the Bratunac Crisis Staff?

utterances.speaker: SRBISLAV DAVIDOVIC
utterances.text: I wouldn't know because I did not take part in the work of either the Crisis Staff or politics at that time. Probably yes, but I am unaware of it. It seems logical that it was held, because Goran was not just anybody. Along with Deronjic, he was the top person in the region. He used to be an MP and a municipal court judge before the war. He was held in high esteem and respected by both the Serbs and the Muslims. The Muslims respected him too until this happened.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Another intervention. It's not that they took his opinion into account, but they had a high esteem for him. The witness could be asked what he meant. Did he actually mean that they respected him?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Well, that's precisely what I meant, held in high esteem, well respected. They appreciated his professionalism, intelligence, loyalty, et cetera.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Mr. Karadzic, it's sufficient for you to raise a certain issue with respect to interpretation. The CLSS will take a look into the matter again. Let's proceed.

utterances.speaker: MS. WEST
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MS. WEST
utterances.text: Sir, today at page 28, you said that the Glogova attack -- you said Glogova was in response to -- to the Goran Zekic killing. Do you remember that? Do you remember saying that today?

utterances.speaker: SRBISLAV DAVIDOVIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. WEST
utterances.text: How do you know that?

utterances.speaker: SRBISLAV DAVIDOVIC
utterances.text: Well, I know that from talking to Deronjic.

utterances.speaker: MS. WEST
utterances.text: Is it possible that the Glogova operation had been planned in advance and it was just accelerated by the Zekic killing?

utterances.speaker: SRBISLAV DAVIDOVIC
utterances.text: It could be put that way.

utterances.speaker: MS. WEST
utterances.text: Mr. President, I'm finished with these particular questions, and I just have one more brief area.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. WEST
utterances.text: Sir, today, beginning at about page 60, you were talking about Rajko Dukic, who was a gentleman from Milici, and there was a discussion about the buses showing up on July 13th in Bratunac. And that Deronjic was angry because he thought Dukic was trying to -- I think what you said, take the burden off his back and put it on someone else's back. Do you remember that testimony?

utterances.speaker: SRBISLAV DAVIDOVIC
utterances.text: I do. But that was on the 12th, that with the buses, not the 13th.

utterances.speaker: MS. WEST
utterances.text: Okay. But is it your remember -- excuse me. Is it your memory that the buses left the next morning, whatever day it was?

utterances.speaker: SRBISLAV DAVIDOVIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. WEST
utterances.text: Now, you also said today at page 58 that after you had this discussion with Deronjic, you said: "Miroslav, try to use your contacts with the government or the president and have the bus and the people taken out of Bratunac." Now, when you said "the president, "you meant Mr. Karadzic; correct?

utterances.speaker: SRBISLAV DAVIDOVIC
utterances.text: Now that -- did I mean him in particular? Well, I meant the top of the party itself and of government. The top people with whom he communicated, with the top people in the political party and in government, because he's the only one of us who had this communication with them.

utterances.speaker: MS. WEST
utterances.text: Well, the top -- the top would be Mr. Karadzic, would it not?

utterances.speaker: MR. ROBINSON
utterances.text: Excuse me, Mr. President. That's the second leading question in a row. I object to that.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Yes. Mr. Davidovic, who was that, the top person?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] President Radovan Karadzic.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MS. WEST
utterances.text: Mr. President, I don't have any further questions.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Thank you. Ms. West, do you have the indictment with you? No? Indictment against Mr. Karadzic. Schedule E lists various Srebrenica killings. Number 15.1, page 23 refers to killing of 50 or more Bosnian Muslim men inside and outside the Vuk Karadzic elementary school and in the surrounding area. What killings do these refer to, just roughly? Killing out -- inside, outside the Vuk Karadzic elementary school and in the surrounding area, what does -- what do you mean "in the surrounding area?"

utterances.speaker: MS. WEST
utterances.text: Mr. President, may I get back to you? I want to be absolutely specific about that.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: No, I'm asking because to know -- in order to know whether the victims of these incident, Schedule 15.1, would include Mr. Rasid Sinanovic whom Mr. Davidovic referred to.

utterances.speaker: MS. WEST
utterances.text: That particular example, no, it would not.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: I won't pose a question about that.

utterances.speaker: MS. WEST
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Then, Mr. Davidovic, unless my colleagues have a question for you, your evidence is concluded. On behalf of this Trial Chamber and the Tribunal as a whole, I thank you for your coming to The Hague to give it, and I also would like to commend your decision to give evidence in public. I hope everything is well with you, and please have a safe journey back home. Thank you again.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I hope so too. Thank you as well.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: So, Ms. West, I take it that his previous testimony can be admitted publicly in its entirety.

utterances.speaker: MS. WEST
utterances.text: We are still grappling about that, and if I could just have until tomorrow morning to give you an answer or our position on that.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Yes. We discussed a lot of portions publicly, which were discussed in private session in the previous case.

utterances.speaker: MS. WEST
utterances.text: I think the only issue is that the -- or the only question would be that the Appeals Chamber did not -- there is no order that specifically allows that transcript to be open, and that's why I pause.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Very well. Is it practicable to continue with the next witness? Is he waiting outside? Yes. Then let's bring him in. So the next witness is Mr. Katanic, and he's going to testify pursuant to Rule 92 ter.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Good afternoon, Mr. Katanic.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Good afternoon.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Would you take the solemn declaration, please.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I solemnly declare that I will speak the truth, the whole truth, and nothing but the truth.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Thank you. Please be seated. Yes, Ms. West.

utterances.speaker: MS. WEST
utterances.text: May I have 65 ter 90304, please.

utterances.speaker: MS. WEST
utterances.text: Sir, what is your name?

utterances.speaker: MILENKO KATANIC
utterances.text: Yes? My name is Milenko Katanic.

utterances.speaker: MS. WEST
utterances.text: Where were you born?

utterances.speaker: MILENKO KATANIC
utterances.text: I was born in Bratunac.

utterances.speaker: MS. WEST
utterances.text: And where do you live now?

utterances.speaker: MILENKO KATANIC
utterances.text: I live in Bratunac now as well.

utterances.speaker: MS. WEST
utterances.text: Sir, an amalgamated statement was prepared containing relevant portions of your OTP statement from November 2008 and your OTP interview from May 2011, and this statement, which is on the screen before you now, is this the one you reviewed and signed in October of 2011?

utterances.speaker: MILENKO KATANIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. WEST
utterances.text: When I reviewed this statement with you a few days ago, you noted to me a correction you wanted to make; right?

utterances.speaker: MILENKO KATANIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. WEST
utterances.text: And specifically, that correction was related to paragraph 26, which regarded the events in Glogova in May of 1992. That's paragraph 26. And you said that you could not characterise or describe those events as a "attack." You said it was an operation to surround Glogova and disarm the people. The operation was done to disarm the village of Glogova. Now, sir, with that correction in place, can you confirm that the statement otherwise accurately reflects an amalgamation of the information you provided the Prosecution?

utterances.speaker: MILENKO KATANIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. WEST
utterances.text: And if you were asked today about the same matters contained in the statement, would you provide the same information to the Trial Chamber?

utterances.speaker: MILENKO KATANIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. WEST
utterances.text: Mr. President, I would tender the statement, and at this point I think there are only six associated exhibits.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Let's -- let us admit the statement first.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: Exhibit P4374, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: I'm not sure he -- what he said about 65 ter 23556 in -- in paragraph 100.

utterances.speaker: MS. WEST
utterances.text: I can address that with him if you allow me.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Yes. Except for that, are there any objections, Mr. Robinson?

utterances.speaker: MR. ROBINSON
utterances.text: No, Mr. President, and we also don't object to adding some of these documents to the list.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Thank you. So all the other associated exhibits will be admitted and be given number in due course. Yes, Ms. West.

utterances.speaker: MS. WEST
utterances.text: Thank you. If I may read a summary. Milenko Katanic was born in Bratunac, continuing to live and work there throughout the war. He attended the first meeting of the initial board of the SDS in Bratunac on August 8, 1990, along with 50 other distinguished locals from Bratunac. At that meeting, Miroslav Deronjic was elected president, and Mr. Katanic was elected treasurer. In the lead-up to the war, Mr. Katanic remained a faithful member of the SDS. He was present when the local Crisis Staff was formed as directed in Variants A and B and during this time there was always someone present at the Bratunac SDS offices, whether day or night. This was ordered by the instructions of December 19th so that if anything bad happened the local office could alert other SDS members. On 24 February, 1992, he attended a meeting of the Municipal Board, and at the meeting Miroslav Deronjic told the SDS members that they had to move on to level two of the instructions into the state of emergency. He told them Bratunac had to implement level two because it was an order. Katanic noted that in April 1992, despite the Crisis Staff of Bratunac issuing a general order on disarmament, in practice only the Muslims were being disarmed. Previously, Miroslav Deronjic and the SDS had armed the Serb population of Bratunac. Mr. Katanic himself had received a rifle. The decision on the operation on the Muslim village of Glogova was made before the death of Goran Zekic. Mr. Katanic thinks that Zekic's death accelerated the date of the attack. The operation itself was planned earlier. As a member of the TO, the witness participated in the operation, and from the way the operation unfolded, Mr. Katanic realised that all parts of the TO and other formations had their own tasks and assignments, working in co-ordination on Glogova. He agrees that the action like those in Glogova and Suha could be concluded to be forcible displacement of the Muslim population. In 1993, Mr. Katanic became the technical secretary of the Bratunac SDS and worked in the party office. He was present at meetings with Deronjic following the fall of Srebrenica in 1995. And in fact, through the lead-up to the war and during it, Mr. Katanic and Deronjic remained close friends. On July 11th, 1995, Deronjic called Katanic and told him about Deronjic's appointment by Karadzic as civilian commissioner for Srebrenica. Deronjic called Mr. Katanic into his office and told him to organise a meeting with Serb representatives from Srebrenica who were on the SDS board. Mr. Katanic brought them together for this meeting at the SDS office, and Deronjic informed everyone that he had been appointed commissioner. At this meeting where Mr. Katanic was present, Deronjic spoke to Karadzic on the phone. The call was put on speaker phone so everyone present could hear. Karadzic said, "Miroslav, you are directly responsible with your life for all civilian affairs in Srebrenica. Your people will be directly responsible to you." Deronjic turned to the SDS members present, including Mr. Katanic, and said, "You have the same responsibilities to me as I have to Karadzic." On the days following the fall the Srebrenica, Mr. Katanic saw Momir Nikolic and Dragomir Vasic at the SDS office in Bratunac. They were present on the 12th and other days afterward. When they arrived on the 12th, Deronjic was also present and the three men talked. Mr. Katanic was present for several phone calls between Deronjic and Karadzic at this time, and Deronjic had almost daily telephone communications with Karadzic, both from the SDS office and elsewhere. He would often comment that he spoke with Karadzic about current events -- with Deronjic, that is. Deronjic had a custom of saying to the wider public, "I spoke with Karadzic today." This was true throughout the period in July from the beginning of the Srebrenica operation through Karadzic's visit to Srebrenica later in 1995. Specifically, Mr. Katanic thinks that Deronjic reported to Karadzic the killings on -- of July 13th at the Kravica warehouse. From Mr. Katanic's understanding, based on as much as he knew about Deronjic, Deronjic would have reported that. Mr. Katanic himself thinks that he heard about the Kravica warehouse killings from Deronjic on the evening of the 13th. And Katanic was told by Deronjic about Muslim prisoners brought from Milici and other municipalities to Bratunac. Deronjic had a conversation about these prisoners with Colonel Beara. Katanic saw Beara in the SDS office on the night of the 13th, making several phone calls. He was giving orders to lower officers talking about fuel. The next day Katanic saw Beara leave Deronjic's office. Deronjic told Katanic that Beara had earlier commanded his subordinates to search for places in Bratunac to imprison Muslims from Srebrenica. There were so many prisoners that Bratunac was unable to hold them all. Mr. Katanic thinks that Deronjic and Karadzic worked together to relocate the prisoners from Bratunac so they would not be killed there. When Karadzic came to visit Srebrenica in August of 1995, Karadzic and Deronjic had a meeting together. Your Honour, that would be the summary.

utterances.speaker: MS. WEST
utterances.text: Mr. Katanic, when did you first meet Miroslav Deronjic?

utterances.speaker: MILENKO KATANIC
utterances.text: Miroslav Deronjic was my age, so I had known him since childhood. We were friends when we were children. We are of the same age. We went to school together, and when we grew up, we shared the same hobbies. We went fishing at the Drina. We played cards. So you can say that I knew him all my life.

utterances.speaker: MS. WEST
utterances.text: And how close was your relationship?

utterances.speaker: MILENKO KATANIC
utterances.text: Well, we were quite close. You can say that we were friends.

utterances.speaker: MS. WEST
utterances.text: And how often did the two of you speak?

utterances.speaker: MILENKO KATANIC
utterances.text: Well, these were not any kind of official talks. We talked in our free time as two friends who socialised.

utterances.speaker: MS. WEST
utterances.text: Was there any particular place that the two of you frequented together to talk?

utterances.speaker: MILENKO KATANIC
utterances.text: In 1992, I opened a cafe that was called Caesar in January. That was the place where we would met the most often and socialise. We spent our free time there. In the evening when we were free, we would always meet up there and exchange views.

utterances.speaker: MS. WEST
utterances.text: And prior to your opening of that cafe, where did you meet before that? Was there another place?

utterances.speaker: MILENKO KATANIC
utterances.text: Well, in the summer, usually it was the motel by the Drina. In wintertime and in the evenings, at the Fontana Hotel.

utterances.speaker: MS. WEST
utterances.text: Did you know his family?

utterances.speaker: MILENKO KATANIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. WEST
utterances.text: And did he know yours?

utterances.speaker: MILENKO KATANIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. WEST
utterances.text: Sir, do you have a nickname?

utterances.speaker: MILENKO KATANIC
utterances.text: Well, I do. Mikan is my nickname. However, I have a nickname that only three persons have ever used, my mother, Deronjic, and that meant a great deal to me. They called me Mice. The third person who used that nickname was a neighbour. That is the nickname that was used by people to whom I was really close in their hearts. That was my understanding of it.

utterances.speaker: MS. WEST
utterances.text: Mr. President, I wonder if this might be a good time to stop.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Very well. Mr. Katanic, we'll adjourn for today and resume tomorrow at 9.00.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
